docs.title: Solar Radio Interferometer (30.0 – 40.0 MHz)
docs.text:
Weekly Report: Week 5 (05.10.2026 – 11.10.2026)

Current Focus: RF Switch Matrix VNA Validation & Backend Integration Jump to Weekly Log

A real-time, dual-channel coherent radio interferometer designed for decametric solar radio burst observation (Solar Type II and Type III events) across the 30.0 – 40.0 MHz band using synchronized SDRplay RSPdx receivers and Raspberry Pi 5.

docs.title: 1. System Overview & Architecture
docs.text: The instrumentation is designed as a high-performance, phase-coherent radio astronomy instrument centered around a dedicated Hardware RF/Clock Front-End and an Embedded Edge DSP Backend (Raspberry Pi 5). The architecture ingests dual continuous baseband I/Q streams at an aggregate bandwidth of \(80\text{ MB/s}\) (\(640\text{ Mbps}\)), enforces integer-sample alignment in real time, and computes the cross-power visibility spectrum via an embedded FX Correlator before streaming compressed spectral frames to a lightweight remote visualization client.

docs.title: 2. Key Engineering Challenges & Design Rationale
docs.text:
Building a coherent radio interferometer with low-cost commercial SDRs presents fundamental physics and timing bottlenecks:

  • Eliminating Sampling Drift with 24 MHz Reference Locking: Independent on-board TCXOs exhibit fractional frequency offsets of a few Hz, causing continuous sample drift (\(k = 0 \to \pm 1 \to \pm 2\dots\)) within seconds. Distributing an external 24.0 MHz clock to both REFin ports forces identical ADC sampling rates (\(f_{s1} = f_{s2}\)), ensuring zero drift over extended observation runs.

  • Broadband Noise Standard for Multi-Tier Calibration: Rather than relying on single-tone CW signals—which introduce periodic phase ambiguity and low correlation contrast—the system integrates a broadband avalanche noise source as an absolute physical calibration standard. This hardware reference fulfills three critical calibration functions:

    1. Coarse Delay Synchronization: Exploits high random entropy across 10 MHz to compress cross-correlation into an isolated Dirac delta (\(\delta[k]\)), driving Peak-to-Noise Ratio (PNR) above 30 dB for deterministic \(k=0\) sample locking.
    2. Instrumental Phase & Gain Equalization: Directly measures the static inter-channel transfer function \(\Delta\phi_0(f)\) across all 2048 FFT bins, establishing the phase calibration matrix to neutralize internal analog filter and path discrepancies.
    3. Radiometric Flux Scaling (\(T_{\text{sys}}\)): Serves as a calibrated hot/cold standard for Y-factor measurements, mapping arbitrary ADC digital units to physical brightness temperature (Kelvin) and Solar Flux Units (SFU) while tracking receiver thermal gain drift.
  • Multi-Process USB Jitter Elimination: API initialization jitter between separate child processes introduces up to \(\sim 30\text{ ms}\) (\(\sim 300,000\text{ samples}\) at 10 MSPS) of startup skew—far exceeding the \(N = 65,536\) FFT snapshot window. A shared-memory barrier gate synchronizes the write-pointers at a common microsecond epoch prior to correlation.

docs.title: 4. Documentation Map
docs.text:
Note: Hardware and firmware implementations are continuously evolving in the lab. Documentation status is tracked below.

Detailed technical documentation, mathematical derivations, schematics, and lab test reports are maintained in the docs/ directory:

  • Hardware & RF Front-End (docs/01-hardware/):

    • RF Front-End & Antennas [Work in Progress]: Antenna geometry, coaxial impedance matching, and BNC Port C termination.
    • 24 MHz Clock Distribution [Work in Progress]: Reference oscillator splitting, phase locking, and REFin port distribution.
    • Avalanche Noise Source [Work in Progress - Updated 21.09.2026]: 2N2222 B-E junction avalanche core, active current mirror biasing, MMIC buffer stage, 10 dB Pi-attenuator matching (-50 dBm output), and GPIO power gating.
    • RF Switching & Routing [Complete - 22.09.2026]: Dual SPDT switches (HMC544AE), symmetric 1:2 resistive Wye splitter, GPIO state control, and port isolation.
    • Host Interconnect & Power [Planned]: Raspberry Pi 5 USB 3.0 throughput constraints, power budgeting, and isolation.

  • Firmware & DSP Pipeline (docs/02-firmware-dsp/):

    • IPC Architecture: Multi-process fork() model, zero-copy POSIX shared memory, and lock-free atomic barriers.
    • Module 1 - SDR Ingestion Driver[Complete - 23.09.2026]: SDRplay API v3 integration and continuous 10 MSPS dual streaming.
    • Module 2 - Real-Time Time Alignment [Work in Progress]: Initial USB startup delay compensation, flush barriers, and sample-level locking (\(k = 0\)).
    • Module 3 - FX Correlator [Work in Progress]: 50% overlap F-Engine, ARM NEON vectorization, Hanning power correction, and Welch integration.
    • Module 4 - UDP Telemetry & Viewer [Work in Progress]: Binary socket protocol and GPU-accelerated PyQtGraph waterfall visualization.
  • Verification & Calibration (docs/03-calibration-tests/):
    • Zero-Baseline Lab Bench Verification [Work in Progress] : CW tone and wideband noise bench tests with peak-to-noise ratio analysis.
    • Debug Chronicles [Planned]: Engineering logbook covering buffer wrap-around, race conditions, and synchronization fixes.
    • Field Deployment [Planned]: Site noise surveys, antenna array erection, and observational campaigns.
  • Deployment Guides (docs/04-deployment-guide/):
    • Raspberry Pi 5 OS Setup [Planned]: Headless Linux tuning, CPU governor optimization, and driver installation.
    • Systemd Daemonization [Planned] Automated boot management, watchdog recovery, and operational scripts.

docs.text:
• End-to-End System Hardware Integration:

    • Integrated all physical sub-modules: 24 MHz reference clock distribution, avalanche noise source, dual-channel RF switching matrix, and dual SDRplay RSPdx receivers.
    • Interfaced hardware control lines with the Raspberry Pi 5 GPIO header (GPIO 6 for RF switch routing and GPIO 26 for noise source DC power gating).

    • Integrated RAII-based GPIO cleanup and POSIX signal handlers (SIGINT/SIGTERM) to ensure fail-safe power shutdown for the noise source.

docs.title: 5.2.1. Current Status: Phase 1 — Lab Benchtop Instrumentation (Completed)
docs.text:
All hardware-level synchronization, real-time shared-memory pipelines, and DSP correlation modules have been validated on the test bench:

  • Clock Phase Coherence: External 24 MHz reference clock distribution verified across both RSPdx ADCs with zero relative sampling drift over 60-second continuous runs.
  • Continuous Dual Ingestion: Multi-process POSIX Shared Memory architecture sustains an aggregate 80 MB/s raw I/Q throughput with zero dropped buffers.
  • Coarse Delay Alignment (Module 2): Automated cross-correlation identifies non-deterministic USB startup offsets and drains buffer lead, locking synchronization to \(\vert{}k\vert{} \le 1\text{ sample}\) (\(\approx 100\text{ ns}\)) with \(\text{PNR} > 15\text{ dB}\).
  • FX Correlation Core (Module 3): Pre-allocated, zero-heap FFTW3 transformation with 50% overlap and Welch integration verified against synthetic and CW bench tones.
  • Real-Time Telemetry & GUI (Module 4): Non-blocking UDP transport with PyQtGraph displaying real-time power spectrum and dynamic waterfall spectrograms.

docs.title: 5.2.2 Future Roadmap: Phase 2 — Field Deployment & Science Archiving
docs.text:
• Automated Calibration Switching: Implement GPIO-driven RF switches to toggle between zero-baseline noise calibration and outdoor antennas.
  • Antenna Field Array: Deploy dual East-West baseline wire dipoles optimized for the 30.0 – 40.0 MHz decametric observation window.
  • Fringe Stopping: Implement continuous sub-sample geometric delay phase rotation (\(e^{-j 2\pi f \tau_g(t)}\)) in the F-Engine.
  • HDF5 Archiving: Integrate rolling daily storage of complex visibilities (\(\text{Re}, \text{Im}, S_{11}, S_{22}\)) in standard HDF5 format on the host workstation.
  • Autonomous Station Automation: Deploy systemd service watchdogs and automated nocturnal cloud backup via rclone.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Raspberry Pi 5 Node: Raspberry Pi OS 64-bit Lite, SDRplay API v3 driver service, FFTW3 (libfftw3-dev), CMake, GCC/G++ with C++17 support.
  • Host PC Node: Python 3.8+, pyqt5, pyqtgraph, numpy.

docs.title: 1. Build and Run Hardware Sanity Check (Raspberry Pi 5)
docs.text:
cd ~/solar_correlator
cmake -B build
cmake --build build -j4

# Restart the SDRplay service and verify dual-device sample lock
sudo systemctl restart sdrplay
./build/alignment_test

docs.title: 2. Launch Real-Time Correlator Backend (Raspberry Pi 5)
docs.text: ./build/solar_correlator

docs.title: 3. Launch Frontend Visualizer (Host PC)

pip install -r viewer/requirements.txt
python viewer/viewer.py

docs.title: Git Version Control & Development Workflow
docs.text: This document defines the version control rules and Git synchronization routines between the Raspberry Pi 5 (Edge DSP Backend), the Host PC (Frontend GUI & Docs), and the GitHub Central Repository.

docs.title: 1. Environment & Architecture
docs.text:
┌──────────────────────────┐
                     │      GitHub Remote       │
                     │  [https://github.com/](https://github.com/)...  │
                     │      (origin/main)       │
                     └─────────────┬────────────┘
                                   │
                ┌──────────────────┴──────────────────┐
                ▼                                     ▼
   ┌──────────────────────────┐          ┌──────────────────────────┐
   │     Host PC (Local)      │          │   Raspberry Pi 5 (SSH)   │

   │ • docs/ (DevLog/Pages)   │          │ • src/ (C++ FX Engine)   │

  • Host PC: Writes documentation (docs/), runs the real-time Python visualizer (viewer/viewer.py), and reviews commits.
  • Raspberry Pi 5: Implements C++ DSP engines, runs driver callbacks, and executes hardware test binaries (tests/).
  • GitHub (origin/main): Central coordination anchor. Code is never transferred directly via raw copy-paste between devices.

docs.title: 3. Core Development Rules
docs.text:
1. Pull First: Always run git pull origin main before touching any code on either device.
  2. Push on Exit: Always commit and push your changes before switching machines.
  3. Inspect State: Run git status before and after staging files to verify what is being included.

docs.title: Scenario A: Developing on Raspberry Pi 5 (C++ Backend)
docs.text:
Run within the remote SSH terminal on the Pi 5 (~/solar_correlator):

# 1. Pull the latest commits pushed from PC
git pull origin main

# 2. Modify files in src/, tests/, or CMakeLists.txt
# Compile and run verification checks
cmake --build build -j4
./build/alignment_test

# 3. Inspect modified workspace
git status

# 4. Stage and commit changes
# Option 1: Existing tracked files only
git commit -am "fix: correct sample lag offset calculation in time_alignment.cpp"

# Option 2: Newly created files included
git add .
git commit -m "feat: implement lock-free queue in ring_buffer.hpp"

# 5. Push upstream to GitHub
git push origin main

docs.title: Scenario B: Developing on Host PC (Python GUI & Documentation)
docs.text:
Run inside Git Bash or terminal on the Host PC:

# 1. Fetch latest backend updates from the Pi 5
git pull origin main

# 2. Edit viewer/viewer.py or documentation in docs/
# Preview markdown changes locally

# 3. Check modified files
git status

# 4. Stage, commit, and push
git add docs/ viewer/
git commit -m "docs: document module 2 sample alignment and PNR threshold results"

# 5. Push to GitHub (triggers GitHub Pages automated build)
git push origin main

docs.title: Issue 1: [rejected - non-fast-forward] (Forgot to Push on Machine A)
docs.text:
You committed on Machine A but forgot to push. Then you made commits on Machine B and pushed. When pushing from Machine A, Git rejects the upload.

Fix: 

# Pull remote commits and rebase your local work on top
git pull --rebase origin main

# Push the rebased commits cleanly
git push origin main

docs.title: Issue 2: "Your branch is ahead of 'origin/main' by N commits"
docs.text:
Local commits were recorded, but they have not been uploaded to GitHub.

Fix: 

git push origin main

docs.title: Issue 3: Newly Created File Ignored by git commit -am
docs.text:
The -a flag only stages files that Git is already tracking. Newly created files are untracked.

Fix: 

git add path/to/new_file.cpp
git commit -m "feat: add new module file"
git push origin main

docs.title: Issue 4: Accidentally Staged Binary or Test Files
docs.text:
You ran git add . and caught large test logs (.dat) or build artifacts (build/).

Fix: 

# Unstage everything without losing code modifications
git reset

# Verify .gitignore covers the files, then stage clean files
git add src/ tests/ docs/ viewer/

docs.title: 7. Commit Message Convention
docs.text:
Maintain clear, structured commit prefixes for clean project tracking:

  • feat: New feature or processing engine (e.g., feat: add Welch accumulation to FX correlator).
  • fix: Bug fix or calibration tweak (e.g., fix: invert buffer drain lag index in alignment loop).
  • docs: Documentation or DevLog updates (e.g., docs: record module 2 zero-baseline test notes).
  • test: Hardware test scripts or harnesses (e.g., test: add 60-second stability check to alignment_test).
  • refactor: Structural code adjustments without logic changes (e.g., refactor: extract constants into config.hpp).

docs.title: Dual-Channel 24 MHz PLL Clock Distribution Subsystem (10 MHz GPSDO Reference)
1.1. Role of Synchronized Clock Distribution in Decametric Radio Interferometry
docs.text:
In a dual-channel radio interferometer observing decametric solar emissions across the 30.0 – 40.0 MHz band, interferometric cross-correlation relies fundamentally on spatial and temporal phase coherence between the two receive paths. When utilizing independent Software-Defined Radios (such as two SDRplay RSPdx units) on separate USB interfaces, independent onboard crystal oscillators (TCXOs) experience relative phase drift, thermal wander, and fractional frequency offsets. These instabilities degrade fringe visibility and disrupt the cross-correlation phase:

\[C_{12}(t) = \langle x_1(t) x_2^*(t) \rangle e^{j \Delta\phi_{\text{drift}}(t)}\]

To maintain \(\Delta\phi_{\text{drift}}(t) \approx 0\) over long integration cycles, both SDRs must be disciplined by a common, ultra-stable master reference clock. The SDRplay RSPdx master architecture operates on a 24.0 MHz reference clock.

This module provides the precision frequency synthesis bridge:

  1. Ingests a 10.0 MHz sinusoidal reference from an external GPS Disciplined Oscillator (GPSDO).

  2. Converts and multiplies the frequency by a rational factor: \(\frac{f_{\text{out}}}{f_{\text{in}}} = \frac{24.0\text{ MHz}}{10.0\text{ MHz}} = \frac{12}{5} = 2.4\)

  3. Splits and conditions the synthesized 24.0 MHz signal into two isolated, low-distortion, \(50\ \Omega\) matched channels feeding SDR Channel A and SDR Channel B.

  4. Integrates an onboard Microcontroller Unit (MCU) for autonomous PLL programming, lock status supervision, and telemetry reporting to the host processor.

docs.title: 2.1. Active PLL Frequency Synthesizer Selection: Analog Devices ADF4002BRUZ
docs.text: Figure 2.1.1: ADF4002 PLL Core and Passive Loop Filter Sub-circuit

docs.title: 2.1.1. Engineering Rationale and Core Selection Criteria
docs.text:
To synthesize a coherent, low-jitter \(24.0\text{ MHz}\) reference clock for the dual SDRplay RSPdx digitizers from an external \(10.0\text{ MHz}\) GPSDO reference, an integer-N Phase-Locked Loop (PLL) frequency synthesizer core is required. The Analog Devices ADF4002BRUZ (16-lead TSSOP package) was selected as the central phase-frequency detector (PFD) and frequency translator.

The design decision is justified across five primary engineering criteria tailored to radio interferometric requirements:

  1. Native External VCXO Architecture & Hardware Customizability: Unlike general-purpose clock generators or RF synthesizers that embed on-chip LC/ring voltage-controlled oscillators, the ADF4002 is specifically engineered as a dedicated PFD/Charge Pump core designed to drive an external Voltage-Controlled Crystal Oscillator (VCXO). This architectural separation grants full customization flexibility:

  2. Custom Pulling Range & Damping: Engineers can freely select an application-specific \(24.0\text{ MHz}\) quartz crystal oscillator with an optimal pulling range (e.g., \(\pm 50\text{ ppm}\) to \(\pm 100\text{ ppm}\)) and tailor the tuning sensitivity (\(K_v\) in \(\text{kHz/V}\)) to match the charge pump voltage swing (\(0\text{V} \dots 3.3\text{V}\)).

  3. Superior Loaded Q-Factor: High-\(Q\) bulk acoustic wave quartz resonators exhibit loaded quality factors orders of magnitude higher (\(Q > 10^4\)) than integrated semiconductor inductors (\(Q \approx 10 \dots 20\)), drastically suppressing broadband thermal noise floor.

  4. Inherent Spectral Purity & Zero Fractional Spurious Products: Converting \(10.0\text{ MHz}\) to \(24.0\text{ MHz}\) yields an exact integer-ratio common divisor:

$$ \begin{gathered} \text{GCD}(10.0\text{ MHz}, 24.0\text{ MHz}) = 2.0\text{ MHz} \ R = \frac{10.0\text{ MHz}}{2.0\text{ MHz}} = 5, \qquad N = \frac{24.0\text{ MHz}}{2.0\text{ MHz}} = 12 \ f_{\text{PFD}} = \frac{f_{\text{ref}}}{R} = \frac{10.0\text{ MHz}}{5} = 2.0\text{ MHz} \end{gathered} $$

  1. Integrated Hardware Lock Detection via Multi-Function MUXOUT Pin: The ADF4002 incorporates an onboard precision digital lock detector accessible via the MUXOUT pin, eliminating the need for external analog window comparators or complex envelope detectors:
  2. Deterministic Digital Threshold: When the phase error between the reference and feedback clocks remains below \(15\text{ ns}\) for 5 consecutive PFD cycles (\(2.5\ \mu\text{s}\) window at \(f_{\text{PFD}} = 2.0\text{ MHz}\)), MUXOUT asserts logic HIGH (\(+3.3\text{V}\)).

  3. Fail-Closed Hardware Gating: The pin directly drives a status LED for physical visual inspection and connects to a hardware external interrupt (EXTI) pin on the supervisory MCU. Any loss of phase lock instantly alerts the edge processor (\(< 1\ \mu\text{s}\) latency) to trip a Fail-Closed safety shutdown, halting digital correlation to prevent corrupted data ingestion.

  4. Zero-Cost, Industry-Standard Modeling via ADIsimPLL™: Development risk and prototyping turnaround are minimized by native integration with Analog Devices' proprietary, free simulation suite ADIsimPLL™:

  5. Full Closed-Loop Synthesis: Cycle-accurate modeling calculates exact passive loop filter component values (\(R_1, C_1, C_2, R_2, C_3\)), predicting phase margin, loop bandwidth, frequency acquisition time, and transient damping without empirical guesswork.

  6. Realistic Phase Noise Summation: The software accurately models the composite phase noise curve by summing the thermal/flicker noise of the \(10\text{ MHz}\) GPSDO, the ADF4002 charge pump FOM, the passive filter Johnson noise, and the \(24\text{ MHz}\) VCXO open-loop phase noise.

  7. Extensive Community Adoption and Proven Reliability: The ADF4001/ADF4002 family represents the standard benchmark across amateur radio (HAM), laboratory frequency standards, GPSDO clean-up loops, and radio astronomy instrumentation worldwide. Its register map, SPI timing characteristics, and layout precautions are extensively documented in peer-reviewed application notes and open-source hardware repositories, ensuring verified design patterns and immediate software library availability.

docs.title: 2.1.2. ADIsimPLL™ Modeling and Loop Filter Synthesis
docs.text:
The loop filter design for the ADF4002 was synthesized in ADIsimPLL™ to achieve an optimal balance between GPSDO long-term tracking and VCXO short-term phase noise cleanup:

  • Loop Bandwidth Optimization: A narrow loop bandwidth (\(f_{\text{BW}} \approx 50\text{ Hz} \dots 100\text{ Hz}\)) was selected. Below \(50\text{ Hz}\), the output clock phase strictly tracks the atomic stability of the GPSDO; above \(100\text{ Hz}\), reference phase noise and PFD switching noise are heavily attenuated, leaving the pristine phase noise of the VCXO crystal to dominate the spectrum.

  • Target Phase Margin: Designed between \(48^\circ\) and \(55^\circ\) to guarantee an unconditionally stable second/third-order passive loop with zero transient ringing and rapid phase settling (\(< 15\text{ ms}\)).

  • Charge Pump Current Configuration: The ADF4002 features an 8-level programmable charge pump (\(0.31\text{ mA} \dots 5.0\text{ mA}\)). Operating nominally at \(I_{\text{CP}} = 2.5\text{ mA}\) provides strong loop gain while allowing dynamic software retuning via SPI if pulling characteristics shift over temperature.

docs.title: 2.1.4. Voltage-Controlled Crystal Oscillator (VCXO) Selection: SX3V24.000B20085F30TNNS
docs.text: The Voltage-Controlled Crystal Oscillator (VCXO) serves as the primary tunable RF actuator within the ADF4002 phase-locked loop. Driven by the filtered analog error voltage (\(V_{\text{tune}}\)) from the passive loop filter, it synthesizes the \(24.000\text{ MHz}\) master clock, feeding both the ADF4002 RF feedback counter (\(R_{\text{FINB}}\)) and the downstream 74LVC distribution buffers.

docs.title: 1. Component Selection Rationale and Architectural Compliance
docs.text:
The design selects the SX3V24.000B20085F30TNNS (24.000 MHz, 3.3V, CMOS output) based on five technical criteria:

  • Compact Form Factor (SMD 3225): Housed in an ultra-compact \(3.2\text{ mm} \times 2.5\text{ mm} \times 1.0\text{ mm}\) 4-pad hermetic ceramic package. Compared to legacy \(7.0\text{ mm} \times 5.0\text{ mm}\) or DIP-14 oscillator modules, this subminiature footprint saves \(> 75\%\) board real estate and minimizes parasitic trace inductance on the high-frequency clock and analog tuning lines.

  • Direct 3.3V CMOS Logic Compatibility: Provides native rail-to-rail HCMOS/LVCMOS output levels (\(V_{\text{OH}} \ge 2.97\text{V}\), \(V_{\text{OL}} \le 0.33\text{V}\) into \(15\text{ pF}\)). This allows direct AC-coupled interfacing to both the ADF4002 input stage and the 74LVC logic buffers without requiring active level-shifting circuitry.

  • Pulling Range & Environmental Stability: Features a nominal pull range (\(\Delta f \ge \pm 50 \dots \pm 100\text{ ppm}\)) across a wide industrial temperature span (\(-40^\circ\text{C} \dots +85^\circ\text{C}\)). This tuning headroom comfortably absorbs initial crystal manufacturing tolerance (\(\pm 20\text{ ppm}\)), solder reflow thermal shock, and multi-year aging offsets, ensuring the ADF4002 can achieve deterministic frequency lock under all ambient field conditions.

  • BOM Cost and Supply Chain Feasibility: Priced at under \(\$1.50\) in prototype quantities, the device avoids the prohibitive cost (\(\$15 \dots \$40\)) of specialized oven-controlled (OCXO) or military-grade VCXOs, satisfying the low-cost requirement of the dual-channel solar interferometer.

docs.title: 2. Engineering Limitation: Absence of Factory \(K_{\text{VCO}}\) Specification
docs.text:
While the manufacturer datasheet guarantees standard digital and quartz metrics (frequency stability, supply current, operating temperature, and minimum pull range), it omits the incremental tuning sensitivity slope (\(K_{\text{VCO}} = \frac{df}{dV_{\text{tune}}}\) in \(\text{kHz/V}\) or \(\text{MHz/V}\)) and its linearity profile across the control voltage span (\(0.0\text{V} \dots 3.3\text{V}\)).

In a charge-pump PLL, the loop bandwidth (\(\omega_n\)) and phase margin (\(\phi_m\)) are directly governed by \(K_{\text{VCO}}\):

\[\omega_n \approx \sqrt{\frac{I_{\text{CP}} \cdot K_{\text{VCO}}}{2\pi \cdot N \cdot (C_1 + C_2)}}\]

An uncharacterized or non-linear \(K_{\text{VCO}}\) presents two primary risks:

  1. Loop Instability: If the actual \(K_{\text{VCO}}\) is significantly higher than assumed, the loop bandwidth widens and the phase margin erodes, risking underdamped ringing or loss of lock.

  2. Phase Noise Peaking: If actual \(K_{\text{VCO}}\) is too low, loop bandwidth contracts, slowing lock acquisition and failing to suppress the crystal's close-in phase noise.

docs.title: 3. Mitigation Strategy and Laboratory Characterization Workflow
docs.text:
To bridge this parameter gap without compromising loop integrity, a two-phase design methodology is implemented:

  • Phase 1: Pre-Layout First-Order Linear Estimation (ADIsimPLL Synthesis): For initial passive loop filter synthesis (\(R_1, C_1, C_2\)), \(K_{\text{VCO}}\) is approximated assuming a linear frequency deviation across an active tuning window of \(\Delta V_{\text{tune}} \approx 2.5\text{V}\) (centered around \(V_{\text{tune}} \approx 1.65\text{V}\)):

$\(K_{\text{VCO, est}} \approx \frac{\Delta f_{\text{pull}}}{\Delta V_{\text{tune}}} = \frac{\pm 50\text{ ppm} \times 24.0\text{ MHz}}{2.5\text{V}} = \frac{\pm 1.20\text{ kHz}}{2.5\text{V}} \approx 0.96\text{ kHz/V} \dots 1.50\text{ kHz/V}\)$

This conservative estimate establishes the baseline capacitor and resistor values in the loop filter.

  • Phase 2: Empirical Bench Extraction in Laboratory Testing (Section 4): During prototype board validation (Section 4), the physical VCXO will undergo open-loop tuning characterization prior to closing the PLL loop:

  • An external low-noise DC source sweeps the \(V_{\text{tune}}\) terminal from \(0.3\text{V}\) to \(3.0\text{V}\) in \(100\text{ mV}\) increments.

  • The output frequency is logged with a high-resolution frequency counter referenced to a 10.0 MHz GPSDO.

  • The incremental sensitivity curve \(K_{\text{VCO}}(V) = \frac{\Delta f}{\Delta V}\) is mapped around the operating midpoint (\(1.65\text{V}\)).

  • The measured \(K_{\text{VCO}}\) value is back-annotated into ADIsimPLL to trim passive filter values (\(R_1, C_2\)) if the actual phase margin deviates from the target \(48^\circ \dots 55^\circ\).

docs.title: 2.1.5. Passive Loop Filter Design and Empirical Optimization via ADIsimPLL™
docs.text: The 3rd-order passive loop filter positioned between the ADF4002 charge pump output (CP) and the VCXO analog tuning input (\(V_{\text{tune}}\)) dictates phase lock acquisition, closed-loop tracking bandwidth, and close-in phase noise suppression. The network was synthesized and iteratively optimized using Analog Devices ADIsimPLL™.

docs.title: 1. Initial Synthesis and Hardware Lock Failure Analysis
docs.text:
In the pre-layout stage, the VCXO tuning slope was theoretically estimated across the nominal \(3.3\text{V}\) tuning window at \(K_{\text{VCO, init}} \approx 889\text{ Hz/V}\).

Figure 2.1.2: Initial Loop Filter Schematic Synthesized in ADIsimPLL (\(K_{\text{VCO}} = 889\text{ Hz/V}\))

Figure 2.1.3: Initial ADIsimPLL Open/Closed-Loop Frequency & Phase Noise Response

  • Initial Synthesized Components: \(C_1 = 5.60\text{ nF}\), \(R_1 = 8.87\text{ k}\Omega\), \(C_2 = 160\text{ nF}\), \(R_2 = 56.2\text{ k}\Omega\), \(C_3 = 820\text{ pF}\), with charge pump current \(I_{\text{CP}} = 5.0\text{ mA}\) (\(R_{\text{set}} = 5.10\text{ k}\Omega\)).

  • Physical Hardware Lock Failure: During initial bench bring-up, the PLL failed to achieve phase lock (MUXOUT Digital Lock Detect remained low). Investigation identified two root causes:

  • VCXO Frequency Drift & Initial Tolerance: The nominal crystal manufacturing offset (\(\pm 20\text{ ppm}\)) combined with thermal drift displaced the free-running frequency outside the capture window of the synthesized filter.

  • Sub-Optimal Pull-in Dynamics: The combination of an under-estimated \(K_{\text{VCO}}\) and an excessively narrow loop bandwidth (\(\approx 501\text{ Hz}\)) restricted the pull-in range, preventing the phase frequency detector (PFD) from steering \(V_{\text{tune}}\) fast enough to acquire lock before phase slips occurred.

docs.title: 2. Empirical \(K_{\text{VCO}}\) Extraction and Loop Bandwidth Optimization (\(f_{\text{BW}} = 2.14\text{ kHz}\))
docs.text:
To establish accurate loop parameters, the physical SX3V24.000B20085F30TNNS VCXO was characterized open-loop on the bench: sweeping \(V_{\text{tune}}\) from \(0.3\text{V}\) to \(3.0\text{V}\) via a low-noise DC source and logging the output with a GPSDO-referenced frequency counter. The actual incremental sensitivity was extracted as:

\[K_{\text{VCO, measured}} = 1.94 \text{ kHz/V} \quad (\approx 2.18\times \text{ higher than the initial } 889\text{ Hz/V} \text{ estimate})\]

With the measured \(K_{\text{VCO}}\), the loop was resynthesized in ADIsimPLL for a target loop bandwidth of \(f_{\text{BW}} = 2.14 \text{ kHz}\) and an optimal phase margin of \(\phi_m \approx 51.4^\circ\).

Technical Rationale for Selecting \(f_{\text{BW}} = 2.14\text{ kHz}\): 1. Robust Acquisition & Thermal Drift Absorption: The capture range expands proportionally with loop bandwidth, while lock time scales inversely (\(T_{\text{lock}} \propto 1/f_{\text{BW}}\)). A \(2.14\text{ kHz}\) bandwidth ensures the loop rapidly absorbs VCXO temperature-induced frequency drift and establishes instantaneous, deterministic lock at power-up. 2. Phase Noise Crossover Optimization: The PFD comparison frequency is \(f_{\text{PFD}} = \frac{10.0\text{ MHz}}{R=5} = 2.0\text{ MHz}\). The \(2.14\text{ kHz}\) boundary marks the optimal crossover point where close-in reference phase noise (tracked inside the loop) intersects the low phase noise floor of the AT-cut quartz crystal (dominant outside the loop). 3. Spur Attenuation Margin: Stability criteria require \(f_{\text{BW}} \le \frac{f_{\text{PFD}}}{10} = 200\text{ kHz}\). Placing \(f_{\text{BW}}\) at \(2.14\text{ kHz}\) provides nearly two decades of frequency separation from \(f_{\text{PFD}}\), allowing the secondary \(R_2 - C_3\) low-pass pole to attenuate charge pump reference spurs below \(-85\text{ dBc}\).

docs.title: 3. Component Standardization (E96 / E24) and \(C_2\) Parallel Synthesis
docs.text:
The theoretical values calculated by ADIsimPLL were mapped to standard commercial SMD 0603 passive components with stable dielectric characteristics:

  • Resistors (EIA E96, \(\pm 1\%\) Metal Film):

  • \(R_1 = 18.0\text{ k}\Omega\)

  • \(R_2 = 33.0\text{ k}\Omega\)

  • Capacitors (EIA E24, C0G/NP0 Dielectric, \(\pm 5\%\)):

  • \(C_1 = 1.00\text{ nF}\) (\(1000\text{ pF}\), low-dielectric absorption)

  • \(C_3 = 220\text{ pF}\)

  • Parallel Capacitor Synthesis for \(C_2\): The exact required integration capacitance is \(C_2 = 11.2\text{ nF}\), a non-standard value in the E24 series. To avoid unstable X7R dielectrics, \(C_2\) is synthesized using two parallel E24 C0G ceramic capacitors:

$\(C_2 = C_{2A} \parallel C_{2B} = 10.0\text{ nF} + 1.20\text{ nF} = 11.20\text{ nF}\)$

Figure 2.1.4: Optimized Loop Filter Schematic with Measured \(K_{\text{VCO}} = 1.94\text{ kHz/V}\) and Standardized E96/E24 Components

Figure 2.1.5: Optimized ADIsimPLL Frequency Response Showing Phase Margin \(> 50^\circ\) and Robust Lock Acquisition

docs.title: 4. Parameter Evolution Summary
docs.text: Loop Parameter / Component Initial Estimate Bench-Optimized Design Functional Role & Engineering Impact VCXO Tuning Gain (\(K_{\text{VCO}}\)) \(889\text{ Hz/V}\) \(1.94\text{ kHz/V}\) Extracted via empirical DC voltage sweep on prototype bench. Loop Bandwidth (\(f_{\text{BW}}\)) \(\approx 501\text{ Hz}\) \(2.14\text{ kHz}\) Broadens pull-in range to absorb crystal frequency drift. Phase Margin (\(\phi_m\)) \(59.4^\circ\) \(51.4^\circ\) Guarantees critical damping with zero \(V_{\text{tune}}\) overshoot. Charge Pump Capacitor (\(C_1\)) \(5.60\text{ nF}\) \(1.00\text{ nF}\) Suppresses initial voltage step transient from CP pulses. Damping Resistor (\(R_1\)) \(8.87\text{ k}\Omega\) \(18.0\text{ k}\Omega\) (E96 1%) Sets loop zero for phase stabilization. Main Integrator Capacitor (\(C_2\)) \(160\text{ nF}\) \(11.2\text{ nF}\) (\(10\text{ nF} \parallel 1.2\text{ nF}\)) Synthesized via dual parallel E24 capacitors for exact value. Spur Suppression Pole (\(R_2 - C_3\)) \(56.2\text{ k}\Omega - 820\text{ pF}\) \(33.0\text{ k}\Omega - 220\text{ pF}\) Suppresses 2.0 MHz PFD switching spurs by \(> 85\text{ dBc}\).

docs.title: 2.2. Supervisory Microcontroller Selection: STMicroelectronics STM32G030J6M6
docs.text: Figure 2.2: STM32G030J6M6 Supervisor MCU, SPI Bus, and SWD Interface

docs.title: 2.2.1. Rationale and Key Technical Features
docs.text:
To configure the ADF4002 frequency synthesizer without driving up manufacturing overhead, the STM32G030J6M6 (ARM Cortex-M0+ @ 64 MHz, 32 KB Flash, 8 KB SRAM) was selected as the onboard supervisor MCU.

The selection is governed by three primary criteria: * Ultra-Compact 8-Pin SO8N Footprint (PCB Cost Reduction): Measuring just \(4.9\text{ mm} \times 3.9\text{ mm}\), the 8-pin package requires minimal board space. This compact profile allows the entire subsystem to fit onto a smaller PCB outline, directly lowering board fabrication and prototyping costs.

  • Dedicated 3-Wire Hardware SPI Interface: The MCU allocates 3 pins for high-speed serial communication (SCLK, MOSI, and LE/CS) to clock the 24-bit configuration latches into the ADF4002 deterministically, avoiding software bit-banging overhead while keeping digital line routing to an absolute minimum.

  • Mature STM32 Ecosystem & Streamlined Debugging: Backed natively by standard tools (STM32CubeIDE, STM32CubeMX, and HAL/LL drivers). Firmware flashing and in-circuit debugging are performed simply over a standard 2-wire Serial Wire Debug (SWD) link with an entry-level ST-Link programmer, ensuring rapid development and straightforward testing.

docs.title: 2.3. Reference Clock Input Conditioning: 10 MHz Sine-to-Square Slicer (REFIN)
docs.text: To synchronize the ADF4002 phase-locked loop to the master timebase of the dual-channel solar interferometer, the board accepts an external \(10.000\text{ MHz}\) reference clock via a female SMA connector (\(J_3\)). This reference is sourced from an external GPS-Disciplined Oscillator (GPSDO) delivering a nominal sinusoidal output across an input dynamic range of \(0.0\text{ dBm} \dots +10.0\text{ dBm}\) into a \(50\ \Omega\) characteristic system impedance.

docs.title: 2.3.1. Technical Rationale & ADF4002 Slew Rate Requirements
docs.text:
The high-frequency input stage of the ADF4002 phase detector (REFIN, Pin 8) comprises an internal AC-coupled comparator biased internally at \(AV_{\text{DD}} / 2 \approx 1.65\text{V}\). The manufacturer specification establishes rigorous operational boundaries for low-frequency reference signals:

Figure 2.3.1: Excerpt from Analog Devices ADF4002 Datasheet Detailing REFIN Input Specifications

  • Datasheet Boundary Constraint: While the REFIN port supports input frequencies from \(20.0\text{ MHz}\) to \(300.0\text{ MHz}\), operation below \(20.0\text{ MHz}\) is officially permitted only if the signal transition speed satisfies:

$\(\text{SR}_{\text{req}} > 50.0\text{ V/}\mu\text{s} \quad (0.050\text{ V/ns})\)$

  • Input Sensitivity Window: \(0.8\text{ V}_{\text{pp}} \dots V_{\text{DD}}\) (\(V_{\text{DD}} = 3.3\text{V}\)), with an input capacitance of \(C_{\text{in}} \approx 10\text{ pF}\).

docs.title: Mathematical Incompatibility of Raw GPSDO Sinusoids:
docs.text:
For a general sinusoidal voltage \(v(t) = V_{\text{peak}} \sin(2\pi f t)\), the maximum slew rate occurs strictly at the zero-crossing points (\(t = 0, \pi, 2\pi\)):

\[\left.\frac{dv}{dt}\right|_{\max} = 2\pi f V_{\text{peak}} = \pi f V_{\text{pp}}\]

Evaluating this physical limit at \(f = 10.0\text{ MHz}\) across the specified GPSDO output power range: 1. Lower Bound (\(P_{\text{in}} = 0.0\text{ dBm}\) into \(50\ \Omega\)): $\(V_{\text{RMS}} = \sqrt{1.0\times 10^{-3}\text{ W} \times 50\ \Omega} \approx 0.2236\text{ V}_{\text{RMS}} \quad \longrightarrow \quad V_{\text{pp}} = 2\sqrt{2} \cdot V_{\text{RMS}} \approx 0.6325\text{ V}_{\text{pp}}\)$

$\(\left.\frac{dv}{dt}\right|_{0\text{ dBm}} = \pi \cdot (10.0\times 10^6\text{ Hz}) \cdot (0.6325\text{ V}) \approx 19.87\times 10^6\text{ V/s} = 19.87\text{ V/}\mu\text{s}\)$

Evaluation: The raw slew rate is \(< 40\%\) of the required \(50\text{ V/}\mu\text{s}\) threshold, severely violating the datasheet boundary. 2. Nominal Field Condition (\(P_{\text{in}} = +7.0\text{ dBm}\) into \(50\ \Omega\)): $\(V_{\text{RMS}} \approx 0.5006\text{ V}_{\text{RMS}} \quad \longrightarrow \quad V_{\text{pp}} \approx 1.416\text{ V}_{\text{pp}} \quad (V_{\text{peak}} \approx 0.708\text{ V})\)$

$\(\left.\frac{dv}{dt}\right|_{+7\text{ dBm}} = 2\pi \cdot (10.0\times 10^6\text{ Hz}) \cdot (0.708\text{ V}) \approx 44.48\text{ V/}\mu\text{s} < 50.0\text{ V/}\mu\text{s}\)$

Evaluation: Even under standard \(+7.0\text{ dBm}\) drive, the transition slope remains below the manufacturer threshold.

docs.title: Physical Consequence of Insufficient Slew Rate:
docs.text:
When an input reference signal traverses the comparator threshold with a slow slew rate (\(< 50\text{ V/}\mu\text{s}\)), internal thermal and semiconductor flicker noise (\(\sigma_v\)) is directly converted into timing uncertainty (aperture phase jitter \(\sigma_t\)) via:

\[\sigma_t = \frac{\sigma_v}{\left.\frac{dv}{dt}\right|_{t=0}}\]

Furthermore, supply ripple or ground bounce can cause multiple false-trigger transitions during a single zero crossing. This creates phase detector cycle slips, erratic phase error voltages, and loss of lock on the ADF4002 digital lock detect circuit (MUXOUT). Therefore, an active Sine-to-Square Slicing Stage is mandatory.

docs.title: 2.3.2. Circuit Topology, BOM Rationalization, and Operational Principle
docs.text:
To convert the slow \(10.0\text{ MHz}\) sinusoid into a fast-edge CMOS digital clock without introducing phase ambiguity, an unbuffered high-speed single inverter configured as a self-biased analog transimpedance amplifier is implemented ahead of the PLL.

Figure 2.3.2: 10 MHz Sine-to-Square Slicer Circuit

docs.title: BOM Optimization Rationale:
docs.text:
Rather than introducing a dedicated RF comparator or specialized clock-squaring IC, the design adopts the SN74LVC1G04DBVR (SOT-23-5). Because 74LVC single-gate logic devices are already present in the system BOM (for complementary RF switch control and clock distribution buffering), utilizing this component achieves two key objectives:

  • Procurement and BOM Consolidation: Minimizes unique component line items, streamlines the supply chain, reduces placement reel setup overhead, and lowers overall assembly cost.

  • Technical Rigor and Jitter Preservation: Standard single-stage CMOS inverters feature an ultra-short propagation delay and an exceptionally low additive jitter floor. When biased as a linear transimpedance stage, the inverter provides high small-signal gain and symmetrical switching without the phase noise degradation common to complex active comparator topologies.

docs.title: Circuit Working Principle:
docs.text:
The conditioning block consists of five coordinated functional elements: 1. \(50\ \Omega\) Broadband Input Termination (\(R_7\)): A high-precision \(49.9\ \Omega\) (0603, \(\pm 1\%\)) thin-film resistor terminates the incoming coaxial transmission line directly at the \(J_3\) launch, absorbing incident RF power and maintaining a return loss \(S_{11} < -25\text{ dB}\) across DC to \(100\text{ MHz}\).

  1. Self-Biased Inverting Slicer Core (\(U_4\) & \(R_4\)): The SN74LVC1G04DBVR inverter is powered from \(+3.3\text{V}\) (\(V_{\text{CC}}\)) and decoupled by \(C_{19} = 1.0\ \mu\text{F}\).

  2. DC Self-Biasing Mechanism: A high-value feedback resistor \(R_4 = 100\text{ k}\Omega\) connects the inverting output (\(Y\), Pin 4) directly to the logic input (\(A\), Pin 2). Because the CMOS gate input resistance exceeds \(10^{12}\ \Omega\), the DC gate current is zero (\(I_{\text{bias}} \approx 0\)). The DC negative feedback forces the quiescent operating point to settle at the exact switching midpoint:

    $\(V_{\text{in, DC}} = V_{\text{out, DC}} = V_{\text{mid}} \approx \frac{V_{\text{CC}}}{2} = \mathbf{1.65\text{V}}\)$

  3. Linear-Region Transconductance Operation: At \(V_{\text{mid}} = 1.65\text{V}\), both the internal PMOS and NMOS channel transistors operate simultaneously in their active saturation regimes. The digital inverter operates as an analog inverting amplifier with an open-loop voltage gain of:

    $\(A_v = -g_m (r_{ds,n} \parallel r_{ds,p}) \approx -20 \dots -35\text{ V/V}\)$

  4. Squaring Action & 50% Symmetry: Even under the minimum specified input drive (\(0.0\text{ dBm} \approx 0.63\text{ V}_{\text{pp}}\)), the small-signal open-loop amplification exceeds \(15\text{ V}_{\text{pp}}\), driving the output stage into rail-to-rail saturation (\(0.0\text{V} \dots 3.3\text{V}\)). Dynamic self-centering at \(V_{\text{CC}}/2\) guarantees an output duty cycle of \(50.0\% \pm 1.0\%\), suppressing even-order harmonic spurs.

docs.title: 2.3.3. Pre-Layout LTspice Verification & Slew Rate Validation
docs.text:
To rigorously confirm that the self-biased inverter circuit satisfies the ADF4002 slew rate threshold across non-ideal interconnect conditions, a transient time-domain simulation was executed in LTspice.

Figure 2.3.3: LTspice Testbench Schematic and Multi-Cycle Transient Response

docs.title: 1. Testbench Configuration
docs.text:
• Signal Source (\(V_3\)): Sourced by SINE(0 0.63 10MEG) AC 1, generating a \(10.0\text{ MHz}\) sine wave with peak amplitude \(V_{\text{peak}} = 0.63\text{V}\) (\(V_{\text{pp}} = 1.26 \text{ V}_{\text{pp}}\), equivalent to \(+0\text{ dBm}\) available drive into \(50\ \Omega\), evaluating upper-margin behavior).

  • Transmission Line & Mismatch Modeling: Sourced through a \(50\ \Omega\) series impedance, traversing an ideal \(50\ \Omega\) coaxial delay line with a propagation delay of \(T_d = 10.0\text{ ns}\) terminated into \(50\ \Omega\).

  • Slicer Model: Evaluated with level-1 behavioral CMOS models (PMOS_LVC and NMOS_LVC) configured for \(3.3\text{V}\) operation, with input DC-blocking capacitor \(1.0\text{ nF}\) and negative feedback resistor \(100\text{ k}\Omega\).

  • Coupling & Load: Output DC blocking is modeled via \(1.0\text{ nF}\) driving a high-impedance load of \(1.0\text{ M}\Omega\) (representing the ADF4002 REFIN input stage).

docs.title: 2. Steady-State Waveform Analysis
docs.text:
As illustrated in Figure 2.3.4 (.tran 0 120n 0 0.1n):

  • Input Waveform (V(n005) — Green Trace): Represents the raw \(10.0\text{ MHz}\) sinusoid arriving across the \(50\ \Omega\) input boundary behind the \(T_d = 10.0\text{ ns}\) transmission line. The signal oscillates symmetrically around \(0.0\text{V}\) with a peak amplitude of \(V_{\text{peak}} \approx \pm 0.33\text{V}\) (\(V_{\text{pp}} \approx 0.66\text{ V}_{\text{pp}}\)), accurately modeling the lower-bound power output of the external GPSDO (\(0.0\text{ dBm} \dots +0.5\text{ dBm}\) into \(50\ \Omega\)).

  • Output Waveform (V(n007) — Blue Trace): Measured at the output of the AC-coupling capacitor (\(C_{22}\)), the conditioned clock settles into a sharp, symmetrical bipolar square wave swinging from \(-1.20\text{V}\) to \(+1.45\text{V}\) (\(V_{\text{pp}} \approx 2.65\text{ V}_{\text{pp}}\)). The positive half-cycle spans exactly from \(t = 60.0\text{ ns}\) to \(t = 110.0\text{ ns}\) (\(\Delta t = 50.0\text{ ns}\)), maintaining a perfectly balanced \(50.0\%\) duty cycle and eliminating even-order harmonic distortion.

Figure 2.3.4: High-Resolution Transient Waveform (\(0\text{ ns} \dots 120\text{ ns}\)) Demonstrating Slew Rate Multiplication Across Zero-Crossing Points

docs.title: 3. Quantitative Slew Rate (\(dv/dt\)) Extraction
docs.text:
A high-resolution inspection of the zero-crossing transitions in Figure 2.3.4 highlights the significant slope multiplication achieved by the self-biased inverter slicer:

  • Raw Input Sine Slew Rate (V(n005) — Green Trace): At the zero-crossing falling edge (\(t = 60.0\text{ ns}\)), the input sinusoid traverses between \(+0.19\text{V}\) (at \(t = 50.0\text{ ns}\)) and \(-0.19\text{V}\) (at \(t = 70.0\text{ ns}\)) over a \(\Delta t = 20.0\text{ ns}\) window:

$\(\left.\frac{dv}{dt}\right|_{\text{input, measured}} = \frac{0.19\text{V} - (-0.19\text{V})}{20.0\text{ ns}} = \frac{0.38\text{V}}{20.0\text{ ns}} = 0.019\text{ V/ns} \equiv 19.0\text{ V/}\mu\text{s}\)$

This measured slope falls far short of the manufacturer's operational threshold, achieving only \(38\%\) of the required \(50.0\text{ V/}\mu\text{s}\) slew rate limit.

  • Conditioned Output Slew Rate (V(n007) — Blue Trace): Triggered synchronously at the input zero crossing (\(t = 60.0\text{ ns}\)), the inverter core vigorously switches states. The output voltage surges from \(-0.60\text{V}\) to \(+0.60\text{V}\) (\(\Delta V = 1.20\text{V}\)) between \(t_1 = 58.5\text{ ns}\) and \(t_2 = 61.5\text{ ns}\) (\(\Delta t = 3.0\text{ ns}\)):

$\(\left.\frac{dv}{dt}\right|_{\text{output, measured}} = \frac{0.60\text{V} - (-0.60\text{V})}{3.0\text{ ns}} = \frac{1.20\text{V}}{3.0\text{ ns}} = 0.400\text{ V/ns} \equiv 400.0\text{ V/}\mu\text{s}\)$

Across the broader linear switching range from \(-0.90\text{V}\) to \(+0.90\text{V}\) (\(\Delta V = 1.80\text{V}\), \(\Delta t \approx 5.0\text{ ns}\)), the average transition speed remains above \(0.360\text{ V/ns}\) (\(360.0\text{ V/}\mu\text{s}\)), with an instantaneous peak derivative at the midpoint reaching \(\approx 0.450\text{ V/ns}\) (\(450.0\text{ V/}\mu\text{s}\)).

This performance provides an \(8\times\) safety margin above the ADF4002 specification (\(\text{SR} > 50\text{ V/}\mu\text{s}\)), ensuring deterministic, jitter-free comparator triggering even under minimal GPSDO input power.

The pre-layout LTspice simulation demonstrates that the self-biased 74LVC1G04 inverter circuit successfully resolves the low-frequency slew rate deficiency of the ADF4002, guaranteeing clean comparator triggering and deterministic phase locking under all operating conditions.

docs.title: 2.4. Square-to-Dual-Sine Conversion and Clock Distribution Topology
2.4.1. Architecture Rationale: CMOS Logic Buffer vs. Dedicated Clock Distributor
docs.text:
To distribute the \(24.0\text{ MHz}\) reference clock from the VCXO core to the two SDRplay RSPdx receiver inputs, the subsystem employs an active splitting and analog wave-shaping network. Rather than using expensive telecom-grade clock distribution ICs (e.g., Analog Devices AD951x or TI LMK series), the architecture implements a low-cost, high-speed CMOS logic buffer topology based on the 74LVC family (SN74LVC2G34 dual buffer or \(2 \times\) SN74LVC1G34 single buffers in SC-70 packages).

Figure 2.4: Dual 74LVC Buffer Splitter, 5th-Order LC Reconstruction Filter, and 6 dB Matching Attenuator

The engineering trade-offs and design justifications are:

  1. BOM Cost & Board Area Optimization:

  2. Dedicated RF clock distribution ICs cost \(\$2.00 \dots \$5.00\) per unit, require bulky multi-pin packages (QFN-16/24), and often introduce I2C/SPI programming dependencies.

  3. The 74LVC logic buffer solution incurs a BOM cost of under \(\$0.20\), occupies a subminiature surface footprint (\(\approx 2.0\text{ mm} \times 2.1\text{ mm}\) for SC-70-6), and operates purely in hardware without supervisory software overhead.

  4. Software-Centric Static Skew Absorption:

  5. Traditional hardware clock trees enforce sub-picosecond trace length matching through differential PECL/LVDS distribution to minimize channel skew.

  6. In this solar interferometer, any static propagation delay mismatch (\(\Delta t_{pd} \approx 50 \dots 150\text{ ps}\), corresponding to \(\Delta\theta < 1.3^\circ\) at \(24.0\text{ MHz}\)) between the buffer gates is absorbed by the backend software pipeline.

docs.title: 2.4.2. Source Termination (\(R_{12} = 22\ \Omega\))
docs.text:
Because the 74LVC gate transitions exhibit sub-nanosecond switching edges (\(t_r, t_f < 1.5\text{ ns}\)), driving high-frequency lines directly into reactive filter networks can induce parasitic edge ringing, ground bounce, and excessive harmonic radiation. At \(V_{\text{CC}} = 3.3\text{V}\), the internal output impedance of a 74LVC driver gate is \(R_{\text{on}} \approx 20\ \Omega \dots 25\ \Omega\). Placing a series damping resistor \(R_{12} = 22\ \Omega\) (0603, 1%) directly adjacent to the buffer output yields:

\[Z_{\text{source}} = R_{\text{on}} + R_{12} \approx 25\ \Omega + 22\ \Omega \approx 47\ \Omega \dots 50\ \Omega\]

This establishes an accurate \(50\ \Omega\) source impedance looking into the subsequent filter, preventing transmission line reflections (\(S_{11} < -20\text{ dB}\)), overshoot, and ringing [00:03:07] (Texas Instruments: PCB Trace Impedance Matching).

docs.title: 2.4.3. 5th-Order LC Butterworth Low-Pass Reconstruction Filter (\(f_c = 30.0\text{ MHz}\))
docs.text:
The external reference clock input of the SDRplay RSPdx requires a clean sinusoidal waveform to prevent clock slicer jitter and internal mixer intermodulation. To convert the \(3.3\text{V}\) square wave into a pure sine wave meeting the Harmonic Suppression \(\le -40\text{ dBc}\) specification, each channel implements a 5th-order passive LC low-pass filter synthesized using the Iowa Hills RF Filter Designer suite:

Figure 2.5: Iowa Hills 5th-Order Butterworth Low-Pass Filter Frequency Response (\(f_c = 30.0\text{ MHz}\), \(-36.9\text{ dB}\) attenuation at \(72.1\text{ MHz}\))

  1. Filter Synthesis & Topology:

  2. Approximation Type: 5-pole Butterworth low-pass filter (maximally flat passband response, zero passband ripple).

  3. Cutoff Frequency: Designed for \(f_c = 30.0\text{ MHz}\) with reference terminations \(R_{\text{Source}} = 50.0\ \Omega\) and \(R_{\text{Load}} = 50.0\ \Omega\).

  4. \(\pi\)-Network Structure:

    • \(C_{29} = 68\text{ pF}\) (Shunt capacitor to ground)

    • \(L_3 = 390\text{ nH}\) (Series inductor)

    • \(C_{30} = 220\text{ pF}\) (Shunt capacitor to ground)

    • \(L_4 = 390\text{ nH}\) (Series inductor)

    • \(C_{31} = 68\text{ pF}\) (Shunt capacitor to ground)

  5. Harmonic Rejection Derivation:

  6. A symmetrical \(24.0\text{ MHz}\) square wave with \(50\%\) duty cycle exhibits intrinsic Fourier harmonic roll-off:

    • Fundamental (\(24.0\text{ MHz}\)): \(0\text{ dBc}\)

    • 3rd Harmonic (\(72.0\text{ MHz}\)): \(20\log_{10}(1/3) \approx -9.54\text{ dBc}\)

    • 5th Harmonic (\(120.0\text{ MHz}\)): \(20\log_{10}(1/5) \approx -13.98\text{ dBc}\)

  7. In Iowa Hills, the 5-pole Butterworth response provides \(-36.9\text{ dB}\) of attenuation at \(72.1\text{ MHz}\) while introducing only \(\approx -0.45\text{ dB}\) of insertion loss at the \(24.0\text{ MHz}\) fundamental.

  8. Net 3rd harmonic suppression delivered to the output:

    $$ \text{Suppression}_{\text{3rd}} = -9.54\text{ dBc} + (-36.9\text{ dB}) - (-0.45\text{ dB}) \approx -46.0\text{ dBc} $$

    This exceeds the \(\le -40\text{ dBc}\) requirement with a \(6.0\text{ dB}\) engineering margin.

  9. High-Frequency Parasitic Mitigation:

  10. Capacitors (\(C_{29}, C_{30}, C_{31}\)): Specified with precision C0G/NP0 dielectric (\(\pm 2\%\), temperature coefficient \(0 \pm 30\text{ ppm/}^\circ\text{C}\)) to prevent thermal phase drift and piezoelectric noise.

  11. Inductors (\(L_3, L_4\)): Implemented with high-\(Q\) ceramic wirewound RF chip inductors (e.g., Coilcraft 0603CS / Murata LQW18AN series, \(Q > 50\) at \(24\text{ MHz}\)). Their high Self-Resonant Frequency (\(\text{SRF} > 600\text{ MHz}\)) ensures inductive behavior persists through the 5th harmonic (\(120\text{ MHz}\)) and beyond.

docs.title: 2.4.4. 6 dB π-Pad Attenuator: Impedance Stabilization, Damping Analysis, and Parameter Synthesis
docs.text: A symmetric 6 dB π-type resistive attenuator pad (\(R_{14} - R_{13} - R_{15}\)) is placed between the 5th-order Butterworth filter and the SMA output port (\(J_5\)). It performs three coupled functions: absorbing out-of-band energy reflected by reactive loads, terminating the Butterworth filter in a constant resistive \(50\ \Omega\) impedance, and conditioning the clock amplitude to match the input window of the SDRplay RSPdx Ref In comparator.

docs.title: 1. Analytical Synthesis of the Symmetric π-Pad Network
docs.text:
For a characteristic system impedance \(Z_0 = 50.0\ \Omega\) and a target attenuation \(A = 6.00\text{ dB}\), the linear voltage attenuation ratio \(k\) is defined as:

\[k = 10^{\frac{A}{20}} = 10^{\frac{6.00}{20}} \approx 1.99526\]

The theoretical values for the shunt resistors (\(R_{\text{shunt}} = R_{14} = R_{15}\)) and series resistor (\(R_{\text{series}} = R_{13}\)) are derived from two-port network transmission parameters:

\[R_{\text{shunt}} = Z_0 \left( \frac{k + 1}{k - 1} \right) = 50.0 \left( \frac{1.99526 + 1}{1.99526 - 1} \right) = 50.0 \left( \frac{2.99526}{0.99526} \right) \approx 150.47\ \Omega\] \[R_{\text{series}} = Z_0 \left( \frac{k^2 - 1}{2k} \right) = 50.0 \left( \frac{1.99526^2 - 1}{2 \cdot 1.99526} \right) = 50.0 \left( \frac{3.98108 - 1}{3.99052} \right) \approx 37.35\ \Omega\]

To guarantee manufacturability and low BOM variance, these parameters are mapped to the closest standard EIA E24 1% tolerance values: * \(R_{14} = R_{15} = 150\ \Omega\) (deviation \(< 0.31\%\))

  • \(R_{13} = 36\ \Omega\) (deviation \(< 3.61\%\))

Evaluating the two-port parameters with standard values yields an actual insertion loss of \(A_{\text{actual}} \approx 6.04\text{ dB}\) and an input return loss of \(S_{11} < -35\text{ dB}\), maintaining an accurate wideband \(50\ \Omega\) port match.

docs.title: 2. Engineering Justification: Selection of 6 dB over 3 dB and 9 dB Alternatives
docs.text:
The selection of a \(6.0\text{ dB}\) attenuation factor represents an optimal engineering compromise between reflection absorption, filter termination stabilization, and comparator slew-rate preservation:

  • Round-Trip Reflection Absorption (12 dB Damping): Because the 5-pole LC Butterworth filter is purely reflective, out-of-band energy reflected by reactive cable interfaces or the receiver's high-impedance clock slicer travels back into the filter network. A \(6\text{ dB}\) pad attenuates these reflections on both the forward and reverse passes (\(2 \times 6\text{ dB} = 12.0\text{ dB}\) round-trip return loss enhancement), absorbing \(> 93.7\%\) of reflected power and eliminating pulse ringing. By contrast, a \(3\text{ dB}\) pad provides only \(6\text{ dB}\) of round-trip damping, allowing \(25\%\) of reflected energy to re-enter the filter and cause group delay peaking.

  • Filter Load Termination Isolation: The pad acts as an impedance buffer, presenting a near-pure \(50.0\ \Omega\) resistive load to the Butterworth filter across all frequencies. This isolates the filter from varying coaxial cable lengths and digitizer input reactance, preventing detuning of the \(30.0\text{ MHz}\) cutoff frequency.

  • Drive Level and Zero-Crossing Slew Rate Optimization: Delivering a clean clock to the SDRplay RSPdx Ref In port requires maximizing the zero-crossing slope (\(dv/dt\)) to minimize aperture jitter without overdriving the input stage. A \(3\text{ dB}\) pad delivers \(\approx 1.5\text{ V}_{\text{pp}}\) (\(+7.5\text{ dBm}\)), which risks overdriving the internal reference slicer and leaking clock harmonics into the RF tuner. Conversely, a \(9\text{ dB}\) pad reduces the delivered amplitude to \(\approx 0.5\text{ V}_{\text{pp}}\) (\(+1.4\text{ dBm}\)); this halves the zero-crossing slew rate (\(dv/dt < 0.04\text{ V/ns}\)), allowing input thermal noise to translate into phase jitter and eroding the \(< 300\text{ fs RMS}\) budget. The \(6\text{ dB}\) pad hits the ideal sweet spot: delivering \(\approx 1.05\text{ V}_{\text{pp}}\) (\(+4.0 \dots +4.5\text{ dBm}\)) with an optimal slew rate of \(\approx 0.08\text{ V/ns}\).

docs.title: 3. Component Power Dissipation and Thermal Derating
docs.text:
To confirm that 0603-size SMD resistors are thermally reliable, power dissipation across each resistor is evaluated under full drive conditions. The signal entering the attenuator pad has an RMS power of \(P_{\text{in}} \approx +10.0\text{ dBm}\) (\(10.0\text{ mW}\)), corresponding to an RMS voltage of \(V_{\text{in, RMS}} \approx 0.707\text{ V}_{\text{RMS}}\) across the pad's \(50\ \Omega\) input impedance: * Shunt Input Resistor (\(R_{14} = 150\ \Omega\)):

$\(P_{R14} = \frac{V_{\text{in, RMS}}^2}{R_{14}} = \frac{(0.707\text{ V})^2}{150\ \Omega} \approx \frac{0.500\text{ V}^2}{150\ \Omega} \approx 3.33\text{ mW}\)$

  • Series Resistor (\(R_{13} = 36\ \Omega\)): The RMS voltage drop across \(R_{13}\) is \(V_{R13} = V_{\text{in, RMS}} - V_{\text{out, RMS}} \approx 0.707\text{ V} - 0.354\text{ V} = 0.353\text{ V}_{\text{RMS}}\): $\(P_{R13} = \frac{V_{R13}^2}{R_{13}} = \frac{(0.353\text{ V})^2}{36\ \Omega} \approx \frac{0.125\text{ V}^2}{36\ \Omega} \approx 3.47\text{ mW}\)$

  • Shunt Output Resistor (\(R_{15} = 150\ \Omega\)):

$\(P_{R15} = \frac{V_{\text{out, RMS}}^2}{R_{15}} = \frac{(0.354\text{ V})^2}{150\ \Omega} \approx \frac{0.125\text{ V}^2}{150\ \Omega} \approx 0.83\text{ mW}\)$

Standard 0603 SMD chip resistors are rated for \(100\text{ mW}\) (\(0.1\text{ W}\)) continuous dissipation. With peak dissipation remaining below \(3.5\text{ mW}\), the resistors operate with a safety factor exceeding \(28\times\), ensuring negligible thermal drift and preventing micro-temperature fluctuations from modulating transmission phase.

docs.title: 2.4.5. Cascaded Output Power Budget, Slew Rate Modeling
docs.text: The cascaded signal path from the 74LVC buffer output through the reconstruction filter, attenuator pad, and TVS clamp establishes an optimized clock signal delivered into the \(50\ \Omega\) load:

docs.title: 1. Stage-by-Stage Power and Voltage Budget
docs.text:
1. CMOS Driver Output Stage: Operating from \(V_{\text{CC}} = 3.3\text{V}\), the 74LVC buffer outputs a rail-to-rail square wave. By Fourier decomposition, the amplitude of the fundamental frequency component is:

$\(V_{\text{fund, peak}} = \frac{4}{\pi} \cdot \frac{V_{\text{pp}}}{2} = \frac{2}{\pi} \cdot 3.30\text{V} \approx 2.101\text{ V}_{\text{peak}} \quad \longrightarrow \quad V_{\text{fund, RMS}} = \frac{2.101}{\sqrt{2}} \approx 1.485\text{ V}_{\text{RMS}}\)$

  1. Source Impedance Voltage Division (\(R_{\text{on}} + R_{12} = 50\ \Omega\) into \(50\ \Omega\) Filter): The internal driver resistance (\(R_{\text{on}} \approx 25\ \Omega\)) combined with damping resistor \(R_{12} = 22\ \Omega\) forms an effective \(Z_{\text{source}} \approx 47\ \Omega \dots 50\ \Omega\). Looking into the \(50\ \Omega\) passband of the Butterworth filter, voltage division halves the fundamental amplitude:

$\(V_{\text{in, filter}} = \frac{1}{2} \cdot V_{\text{fund, peak}} \approx 1.050\text{ V}_{\text{peak}} \quad (0.743\text{ V}_{\text{RMS}})\)$

$\(P_{\text{in, filter}} = 10 \log_{10}\left( \frac{(0.743\text{ V})^2 / 50\ \Omega}{1.0\times 10^{-3}\text{ W}} \right) \approx 10 \log_{10}(11.04\text{ mW}) \approx +10.43\text{ dBm}\)$

  1. 5th-Order LC Butterworth Filter Loss: At \(f = 24.0\text{ MHz}\), passband insertion loss (accounting for inductor ESR and finite capacitor \(Q\)) is:

$\(\Delta S_{21,\text{LPF}} \approx -0.45\text{ dB} \quad \longrightarrow \quad P_{\text{out, LPF}} \approx +10.43 - 0.45 = +9.98\text{ dBm} \quad (\approx 1.99\text{ V}_{\text{pp}})\)$

  1. 6 dB π-Pad Attenuator Loss:

$\(\Delta S_{21,\text{pad}} \approx -6.04\text{ dB} \quad \longrightarrow \quad P_{\text{delivered}} = +9.98 - 6.04 = +3.94\text{ dBm} \approx +4.0 \dots +4.5\text{ dBm}\)$ The resulting RMS and peak-to-peak voltages delivered across the calibrated \(50\ \Omega\) load of the SDRplay RSPdx Ref In port are:

$\(V_{\text{out, RMS}} = \sqrt{10^{\frac{+3.94}{10}} \times 10^{-3}\text{ W} \times 50\ \Omega} \approx \sqrt{0.00248\text{ W} \times 50\ \Omega} \approx 0.352\text{ V}_{\text{RMS}}\)$

$\(V_{\text{out, pp}} = 2\sqrt{2} \cdot V_{\text{out, RMS}} \approx 2.8284 \cdot 0.352\text{ V}_{\text{RMS}} \approx \text{ V}_{\text{pp}} \dots 1.10\text{ V}_{\text{pp}}\)$

docs.title: 2. Zero-Crossing Slew Rate Analysis
docs.text:
The zero-crossing slew rate of the delivered \(24.0\text{ MHz}\) sine wave (\(v(t) = V_{\text{peak}} \sin(2\pi f t)\) with \(V_{\text{peak}} \approx 0.525\text{ V}\)) is calculated as:

\[\left.\frac{dv}{dt}\right|_{t=0} = 2\pi f V_{\text{peak}} = 2\pi \cdot (24.0\times 10^6\text{ Hz}) \cdot 0.525\text{ V} \approx 79.17\times 10^6\text{ V/s} \approx \mathbf{0.0792\text{ V/ns}}\]

This slope ensures that external clock comparators switch crisply across their threshold hysteresis band (\(V_{\text{hyst}} \approx 20\text{ mV}\) is traversed in \(\Delta t < 250\text{ ps}\)), minimizing aperture jitter.

docs.title: 2.4.6. Pre-Layout LTspice Verification: Impedance Mismatch Stress and Transient Dynamics
docs.text:
To validate the operational stability of the 5th-order Butterworth reconstruction filter under severe boundary conditions, a comparative time-domain simulation was executed in LTspice. The testbench directly contrasts an unmitigated filter channel against the 6 dB \(\pi\)-pad attenuated topology when subjected to simultaneous input source mismatch and open-circuit load reflection.

Figure 2.6: LTspice Transient Comparison of Filter Output With vs. Without 6 dB π-Pad Attenuator Under Severe Load Mismatch (\(T_d = 12\text{ ns}\), \(R_{\text{load}} = 1\text{ M}\Omega\))

docs.title: 1. Simulation Testbench Configuration
docs.text:
Both channels evaluate identical 5-pole LC low-pass networks (\(C_1=C_3=C_5=C_7=68\text{ pF}\), \(C_2=C_6=220\text{ pF}\), \(L_1=L_2=L_3=L_4=390\text{ nH}\)) excited by synchronized \(24.0\text{ MHz}\) CMOS pulse generators (\(V_1, V_2\): \(0 \dots 3.3\text{V}\), \(t_r = t_f = 2.0\text{ ns}\), period \(T = 41.667\text{ ns}\)):

  • Source Impedance Mismatch (\(R_2 = R_6 = 38\ \Omega\)): To evaluate filter sensitivity to driver process-voltage-temperature (PVT) variations, the series source resistance is deliberately set to \(38\ \Omega\) ahead of the \(1\text{ nF}\) DC blocking capacitors (\(C_8, C_9\)). This models an under-damped driver state where output impedance deviates from nominal matching.

  • Transmission Line & Open-Circuit Load (\(T_1, T_2\) and \(R_5, R_{10}\)): Each channel drives an ideal \(50\ \Omega\) coaxial transmission line with a one-way delay of \(T_d = 12.0\text{ ns}\) (equivalent to \(\approx 2.4\text{ m}\) of standard RG-58 coaxial cable at \(VF = 0.66\)). The far-end terminations are set to an extreme mismatch of \(R_5 = R_{10} = 1\text{ M}\Omega\), establishing a worst-case reflection coefficient:

$\(\Gamma_L = \frac{10^6 - 50}{10^6 + 50} \approx +1.00\)$

  • Topology Differentiation:

  • Channel 1 (OUT — Green Trace): The LC filter drives the \(12\text{ ns}\) transmission line directly without resistive attenuation.

  • Channel 2 (OUT_TR — Blue Trace): The LC filter drives the line through the \(6\text{ dB}\) \(\pi\)-pad network (\(R_7 = R_9 = 150\ \Omega\), \(R_8 = 36\ \Omega\)).

docs.title: 2. Time-Domain Waveform Analysis and Standing Wave Dynamics
docs.text:
The transient simulation results (.tran 0 1.2u 1u 10p) highlight the contrast between the two network configurations under reflective load stress:

  • Unmitigated Path (V(out) — Green Trace):

  • Standing Wave Resonance: Total round-trip transit time along the transmission line is \(2 \cdot T_d = 24.0\text{ ns}\), representing \(57.6\%\) of the clock period. The undamped reactive LC filter reflects incoming reverse wavefronts back into the line, creating standing waves.

  • Envelope Distortion and Ringing: V(out) exhibits visible harmonic distortion, pronounced shoulder bumps, and significant baseline asymmetry. The peak-to-peak voltage swings uncontrolled from \(-1.55\text{V}\) to \(+3.65\text{V}\) (\(V_{\text{pp}} \approx 5.20\text{ V}_{\text{pp}}\)). Applying this overdriven, ring-distorted waveform to an RSPdx clock slicer would induce comparator threshold hunting, phase jitter, and spurious harmonic mixing.

  • 6 dB Attenuated Path (V(out_tr) — Blue Trace):

  • Reflection Damping: Sourced reflections returning from the \(1\text{ M}\Omega\) boundary are absorbed across \(R_7, R_8,\) and \(R_9\). Any residual wave bouncing off the LC filter is attenuated a second time on the forward pass, attenuating round-trip standing waves.

  • Sinusoidal Purity: The output V(out_tr) emerges as a pure, symmetrical sine wave completely free of ringing, overshoot, or secondary inflection points. Under open-circuit conditions, the swing is bounded to \(-1.20\text{V} \dots +1.25\text{V}\) (\(V_{\text{pp}} \approx 2.45\text{ V}_{\text{pp}}\)), which naturally settles into the target \(\approx 1.05\text{ V}_{\text{pp}}\) (\(+4.4\text{ dBm}\)) when loaded by a nominal \(50\ \Omega\) receiver port.

  • Monotonic Zero-Crossing: The smooth, uninterrupted zero-crossing transition guarantees deterministic triggering for subsequent clock digitizers.

docs.title: 3. Verification Conclusion
docs.text: The LTspice analysis verifies that the 5th-order Butterworth filter maintains harmonic filtering despite driver resistance variations (\(R_{\text{source}} = 38\ \Omega\)). Furthermore, the 6 dB \(\pi\)-pad isolates the filter from line resonances, ensuring clean sinusoidal delivery to the receivers regardless of external cable lengths or load reactance.

docs.title: 2.7. Power Supply and Voltage Regulation Architecture: TI LP5907MFX-3.3/NOPB
docs.text: Figure 2.7: Power Input Protection (SS14) and Ultra-Low-Noise LDO Regulation (LP5907)

docs.title: 2.7.1. Selection Rationale and Current Budget Optimization
docs.text:
The subsystem operates from an external nominal \(+5.0\text{V}\) DC supply and requires a highly stable, low-noise \(+3.3\text{V}\) regulated rail. The Texas Instruments LP5907MFX-3.3/NOPB (ultra-low-noise linear regulator, 250 mA, SOT-23-5) was selected based on three concise criteria:

  • Low Total Current Consumption & Thermal Margin: The aggregate current consumption across all active devices is minimal:
  • ADF4002 PLL Synthesizer: \(\approx 5\text{ mA}\)
  • STM32G030J6M6 MCU: \(\approx 4\text{ mA}\) (idle state after startup configuration)
  • 24.0 MHz VCXO: \(\approx 15\text{ mA}\)
  • 74LVC Clock Buffers: \(\approx 25\text{ mA}\) (dynamic switching into \(50\ \Omega\) loads)
  • Total Current Demand: \(I_{\text{total}} \approx 45 - 55\text{ mA}\). The 250 mA continuous output rating offers over \(4\times\) current headroom. With \(V_{\text{IN}} = 5.0\text{V}\), total package power dissipation is strictly bounded: $\(P_D = (V_{\text{IN}} - V_{\text{OUT}}) \cdot I_{\text{total}} \approx (5.0\text{V} - 3.3\text{V}) \cdot 55\text{ mA} \approx 94\text{ mW}\)$ This low thermal load allows the compact SOT-23-5 package to operate cool without requiring heatsinking or dedicated thermal copper planes.
  • Ultra-Low Noise & High PSRR (Phase Jitter Preservation):
  • Output Noise: Features an ultra-low noise density of \(6.5\ \mu\text{V}_{\text{RMS}}\) (\(10\text{ Hz} \dots 100\text{ kHz}\)) without requiring a bulky external noise-bypass capacitor (\(C_{\text{NR}}\)), minimizing board area.
  • Ripple Rejection: High Power Supply Rejection Ratio (\(\text{PSRR} > 82\text{ dB}\) at \(1\text{ kHz}\), \(> 60\text{ dB}\) at \(100\text{ kHz}\)) effectively attenuates upstream switching regulator ripple and line noise.

docs.title: 2.7.2. Reverse-Polarity Input Protection (SS14 Schottky Diode)
docs.text: To protect active silicon components against accidental reverse connection during field installation: * Series Schottky Clamping: An SS14 Schottky barrier diode (40 V, 1 A, SMA / DO-214AC package) is placed in direct series on the \(+5\text{V}\) input line immediately following the DC terminal block. * Low Forward Voltage Drop (\(V_F\)): At low operating currents (\(I \approx 55\text{ mA}\)), the forward drop across the SS14 is only \(V_F \approx 0.35\text{ V} \dots 0.38\text{ V}\). The voltage delivered to the LDO input remains well above its dropout threshold: $\(V_{\text{IN, LDO}} = 5.0\text{V} - V_F \approx 4.62\text{V} \gg V_{\text{OUT}} + V_{\text{dropout}} = 3.3\text{V} + 0.12\text{V} = 3.42\text{V}\)$ * Fail-Safe Isolation: Under reverse polarity, the SS14 blocks reverse current flow completely, protecting the LDO and all downstream circuits against negative voltage damage.

docs.title: 2.8. Passive Signal Conditioning: AC Coupling, DC Decoupling, and Front-End ESD Protection Network
2.8.1. AC Coupling and DC Blocking Architecture (1000 pF C0G / NP0)
docs.text: To establish galvanic DC isolation between successive active stages while preserving high-frequency transmission integrity, series DC blocking capacitors are inserted along all critical RF and clock paths: * 10 MHz GPSDO Input Path: Isolates external GPSDO ground offsets and DC bias voltages from the sensitive input threshold of the sine-to-square fast slicer. * 24 MHz VCXO Core Output: Blocks the internal DC bias of the oscillator transistor core from entering the CMOS buffer splitters. * Dual 24 MHz Channel Outputs (Ch 1 & Ch 2): Prevents external DC potentials or accidental phantom DC supply from the SDRplay RSPdx bias-T circuits from shorting back into the LC reconstruction filters.

docs.title: 1. Component Selection: Murata GRM1885C1H102JA01D
docs.text: The selected DC blocking element is the Murata GRM1885C1H102JA01D (\(1000\text{ pF} \pm 5\%\), \(50\text{V}\), 0603 footprint / 1608 Metric). The selection is governed by fundamental dielectric physics: * Ultra-Stable C0G/NP0 Dielectric: Unlike general-purpose ferroelectric ceramics (X5R, X7R), Class 1 C0G/NP0 dielectric materials exhibit zero piezoelectric microphonics, zero aging rate, and negligible DC voltage coefficient (capacitance remains strictly constant regardless of DC bias voltage). * Thermal Phase Stability: The temperature coefficient is strictly constrained to \(0 \pm 30\text{ ppm/}^\circ\text{C}\) across \(-55^\circ\text{C} \dots +125^\circ\text{C}\). This guarantees that ambient temperature swings in field deployments will not modulate the insertion phase or create inter-channel phase drift between Output A and Output B.

docs.title: 2. Reactance and Corner Frequency Derivation
docs.text:
In a characteristic \(Z_0 = 50.0\ \Omega\) transmission environment, the capacitive reactance of a \(C_{\text{block}} = 1000\text{ pF}\) (\(1.0\text{ nF}\)) capacitor is: * At Reference Frequency (\(10.0\text{ MHz}\)): $\(X_C(10\text{ MHz}) = \frac{1}{2\pi f C} = \frac{1}{2\pi \cdot 10.0\times 10^6\text{ Hz} \cdot 1.0\times 10^{-9}\text{ F}} \approx 15.92\ \Omega\)$ * At Synthesized Clock Frequency (\(24.0\text{ MHz}\)): $\(X_C(24\text{ MHz}) = \frac{1}{2\pi f C} = \frac{1}{2\pi \cdot 24.0\times 10^6\text{ Hz} \cdot 1.0\times 10^{-9}\text{ F}} \approx 6.63\ \Omega\)$

The high-pass corner frequency (\(-3\text{ dB}\) cutoff) into a terminated \(50\ \Omega\) load is calculated as: $\(f_c = \frac{1}{2\pi R C} = \frac{1}{2\pi \cdot 50\ \Omega \cdot 1.0\times 10^{-9}\text{ F}} \approx 3.183\text{ MHz}\)$

Because \(f_c \approx 3.18\text{ MHz}\) is positioned far below both the \(10.0\text{ MHz}\) reference and the \(24.0\text{ MHz}\) synthesized clock, the insertion attenuation contributed by the capacitor is virtually unmeasurable (\(S_{21} > -0.04\text{ dB}\) at \(24\text{ MHz}\)), introducing zero group delay distortion or pulse-edge degradation into the clock signal.

docs.title: 2.8.2. Power Rail DC Decoupling Architecture (1 µF X7R)
docs.text: Dedicated 1 µF ceramic capacitors (TMK107B7105KA-T, 0603 X7R) are placed at each active supply pin to suppress power rail ripple and deliver instantaneous transient current during high-speed switching of the STM32 MCU and 74LVC clock buffers.

docs.title: 1. Component Selection: Taiyo Yuden TMK107B7105KA-T
docs.text: Every active supply pin (\(V_{\text{DD}}\) of MCU, \(V_{\text{P}}/V_{\text{DD}}\) of ADF4002, \(V_{\text{CC}}\) of VCXO, \(V_{\text{CC}}\) of CMOS buffers, and output nodes of low-noise LDOs) is bypassed by a dedicated TMK107B7105KA-T (\(1.0\ \mu\text{F} \pm 10\%\), \(16\text{V}\), 0603 footprint, X7R dielectric): * DC Bias Derating Resilience: While subminiature ceramic capacitors in 0201 or 0402 footprints lose up to \(60 - 80\%\) of their effective capacitance when operated near their rated voltage, the 0603 footprint with a \(16\text{V}\) rating maintains over \(88\%\) of its nominal capacitance (\(C_{\text{eff}} \approx 0.88\ \mu\text{F}\)) when biased at nominal \(3.3\text{V}\) system rails. * Low Equivalent Series Inductance (ESL): The 0603 SMD packaging restricts parasitic loop inductance to \(\text{ESL} \approx 0.6\text{ nH}\). When mounted with dual ground stitching vias immediately adjacent to component pads, it forms a low-impedance shunt network (\(Z_{\text{rail}} < 0.15\ \Omega\)) spanning from DC up to \(> 15\text{ MHz}\), effectively attenuating charge pump switching transients and digital MCU current steps.

docs.title: 2.8.3. Front-End Transient & ESD Protection (Texas Instruments TPD1E01B04DPYR)
docs.text: Because the 10 MHz reference input and the dual 24 MHz clock outputs interface via external panel SMA connectors and coaxial interconnects, they are routinely exposed to electrostatic discharge (ESD) and human/cable handling discharge events (CDE).

docs.title: 1. Component Selection: Texas Instruments TPD1E01B04DPYR
docs.text: Each external SMA connector center conductor is guarded by a discrete TPD1E01B04DPYR bidirectional TVS protection diode in an ultra-compact X1SON-2 (DPY, 0402 equivalent) package: * IEC 61000-4-2 Level 4 Compliance: Rated to withstand up to \(\pm 15\text{ kV}\) Air-Gap Discharge and \(\pm 15\text{ kV}\) Contact Discharge, providing robust industrial-grade surge suppression. * Ultra-Low Junction Capacitance (\(C_j \approx 0.18\text{ pF}\)): High-frequency clock and RF signals are severely compromised by standard TVS diodes whose parasitic capacitance (\(> 5\text{ pF}\)) shunts high frequencies to ground. The TPD1E01B04 presents an ultra-low capacitance of only \(C_j = 0.18\text{ pF}\) typical (\(0.25\text{ pF}\) maximum).

docs.title: 2. High-Frequency RF Transparency Verification
docs.text:
At the highest operating frequency of the subsystem (\(f = 24.0\text{ MHz}\)), the shunt impedance presented by the TVS junction capacitance is: $\(X_{C,\text{ESD}} = \frac{1}{2\pi \cdot 24.0\times 10^6\text{ Hz} \cdot 0.18\times 10^{-12}\text{ F}} \approx 36.84\text{ k}\Omega\)$

Because \(X_{C,\text{ESD}} \approx 36.8\text{ k}\Omega \gg 50.0\ \Omega\), the parallel loading effect on the \(50\ \Omega\) transmission line is completely negligible: $\(S_{21,\text{loss}} \approx 10\log_{10}\left(1 - \frac{Z_0}{2 \cdot X_{C,\text{ESD}}}\right) \approx 10\log_{10}\left(1 - \frac{50}{73680}\right) \approx -0.0029\text{ dB}\)$

The diode operates completely transparently across both \(10.0\text{ MHz}\) and \(24.0\text{ MHz}\), introducing zero pulse distortion, preserving return loss (\(S_{11} < -45\text{ dB}\)), and introducing no phase imbalance between the dual receiver clock feeds.
