docs.title: 3. PCB Physical Layout and Mixed-Signal Implementation
docs.text: The physical PCB implementation of the Dual-Channel 24 MHz PLL Clock Distribution Subsystem requires strict adherence to modern Analog Mixed-Signal (AMS) and high-frequency RF routing principles. At high switching speeds, parasitic trace inductance, ground return discontinuities, and substrate coupling can degrade phase noise, increase clock jitter, and compromise channel-to-channel isolation. This section details the stackup synthesis, grounding topology, critical signal routing, power distribution, and RF launch geometry designed to preserve signal integrity across the board.

docs.title: 3.1. 4-Layer Stackup Architecture and Controlled Transmission Lines
docs.text:
A dedicated 4-layer stackup on an FR-4 substrate (\(H_{\text{total}} \approx 1.6\text{ mm}\), \(\varepsilon_r \approx 4.4\)) is implemented to establish continuous reference planes and minimize magnetic loop areas:

  • Layer 1 (Top Layer — Primary Signals & RF): Dedicated to high-frequency RF routing, the \(10\text{ MHz}\) reference input, \(24\text{ MHz}\) master clock paths, VCXO loop feedback, and discrete SMD components. All unused surface copper is flooded with a ground plane connected directly to Layer 2 through an array of micro-vias.
  • Layer 2 (Inner Layer 1 — Solid Ground Plane): Configured as an unbroken, continuous ground reference plane (GND) across the entire board boundary. It provides an immediate, low-impedance image plane directly beneath all Layer 1 high-speed conductors.
  • Layer 3 (Inner Layer 2 — Dedicated Power Pours): Configured for DC power distribution, subdivided into isolated, low-impedance copper pours (\(+3.3\text{V}_{\text{ANA}}\), \(+3.3\text{V}_{\text{DIG}}\), and \(+5.0\text{V}_{\text{IN}}\)).
  • Layer 4 (Bottom Layer — Non-Critical Routing): Dedicated to low-speed, non-critical digital interconnects (such as MCU GPIOs, SPI control lines, status LED lines, and debug headers). The entire remaining area is flooded with a solid ground pour to form an external shielding enclosure.

Figure 3.1.1: JLCPCB standard 4-layer stackup configuration (1.6 mm total thickness, 1 oz outer / 0.5 oz inner copper weight, 7628 prepreg).

docs.title: Controlled Impedance Synthesis (\(50\ \Omega\))
docs.text: All RF and high-speed clock traces on Layer 1 are synthesized as Coplanar Waveguides with Ground (CPW-G). The single 7628 prepreg layer between Layer 1 and Layer 2 (\(h = 0.2104\text{ mm}\)) establishes controlled capacitive coupling to the solid ground image plane. Trace width (\(W \approx 0.38\text{ mm}\)) and coplanar ground clearance (\(G \approx 0.25\text{ mm}\)) are synthesized to maintain nominal \(Z_0 = 50.0\ \Omega\) across all critical clock and RF routes..

docs.title: 3.2. Modern Mixed-Signal Grounding Strategy: Unified vs. Split Ground Plane
docs.text:
A critical decision in modern analog mixed-signal layout is the treatment of ground returns. While legacy mixed-signal design guidelines frequently advocated splitting the ground plane into separate Analog Ground (AGND) and Digital Ground (DGND) regions connected at a single star point, this design enforces a single, unified, unbroken ground plane across the entire board.

Figure 3.2: Mastering Split Planes for Clean Power Delivery — Comparison between split ground plane return path discontinuities and unified ground plane spatial zoning.

docs.title: Technical Rationale for a Unified Ground Plane:
docs.text:
1. Elimination of EMI Loop Antennas: At frequencies above \(1\text{ MHz}\), return currents do not take the path of least resistance; they take the path of least inductance, traveling on the reference plane directly beneath the signal trace. If a high-speed digital line crosses a ground plane split, the return current cannot cross the dielectric gap and must detour around the boundary. This detour creates a wide current loop that radiates as an efficient slot antenna, leading to severe electromagnetic interference (EMI) and cross-domain phase jitter.
  2. Spatial Partitioning by Grouping (Zoning): Rather than cutting the copper plane, isolation is achieved through physical placement zoning:
  3. Analog/RF Domain: Grouped exclusively on one side of the PCB (comprising the \(10\text{ MHz}\) input slicer, ADF4002 synthesizer, passive loop filter, \(24\text{ MHz}\) VCXO, and LC reconstruction filters).
  4. Digital Domain: Grouped on the opposing section (comprising the supervisory MCU, SPI lines, debug headers, and LED status logic).
  5. Because return currents remain tightly concentrated beneath their respective conductors, digital switching currents never cross into the analog ground floor, preserving a noise floor \(<-140\text{ dBc/Hz}\).

docs.title: 3.3. Component Placement, Grouping, and Critical Routing Guidelines
3.3.1. Low-Inductance Decoupling Placement
docs.text: Power supply ripple modulates active semiconductor thresholds, resulting in Amplitude Modulation to Phase Modulation (AM-to-PM) conversion. To suppress high-frequency supply spikes: * Placement Proximity: Decoupling capacitors are placed immediately adjacent to the IC supply pins (\(< 1.0\text{ mm}\) spacing). * Inductance Loop Minimization: Vias to the internal power plane (Layer 3) connect first to the capacitor pad before feeding the IC pin, preventing high-frequency noise from bypassing the filtering element. * Direct Ground Return Vias: Ground vias are located immediately adjacent to the capacitor ground pads, routing transient return currents into Layer 2 with minimal loop inductance.

docs.title: 3.3.2. Slew Rate and Trace Length Constraints
docs.text:
• High-Speed Digital Logic: Digital control lines and clock buffer outputs exhibit sub-nanosecond switching edges (\(dv/dt > 1\text{ V/ns}\)), producing high-frequency harmonic energy (\(> 500\text{ MHz}\)). All digital interconnects (MCU SPI bus, buffer drivers) are kept as short as physically possible to reduce capacitive loading and radiated harmonic emissions.
  • Sensitive RF Blocks & VCXO Feedback: While pure analog signals produce fewer high-order harmonics, high-impedance RF nodes are susceptible to parasitic capacitive and inductive picking.
  • Critical VCXO Feedback Route: The \(24.0\text{ MHz}\) feedback line from the VCXO output back to the ADF4002 RF input (\(R_{\text{FINB}}\)) is routed using the shortest possible direct CPW-G line. Parasitic capacitance on this trace directly loads the VCXO crystal tank, while stray inductance can shift loop phase margins, leading to phase instability.

docs.title: 3.3.3. Power Distribution via Copper Pours
docs.text: To maintain low DC series resistance (\(R\)) and negligible parasitic trace inductance (\(L\)), narrow traces are eliminated on the power distribution network. * Dedicated polygon copper pours are utilized on Layer 3 for each regulated voltage domain. * Using broad copper pours lowers the characteristic impedance of the power distribution network (\(Z_{\text{PDN}}\)), preventing dynamic voltage drops (\(V = L \frac{di}{dt}\)) during simultaneous CMOS output switching.

docs.title: 3.4. High-Frequency SMA Launch Geometry and Transition Optimization
docs.text: Standard commercial SMA edge-mount or surface-mount connectors typically feature wide center contact pins designed for 2-layer boards (\(W_{\text{pin}} \approx 1.2\text{ mm} \dots 1.6\text{ mm}\)). On a thin 4-layer stackup where the dielectric height to ground is small (\(h \approx 0.1\text{ mm}\)), such a wide landing pad introduces excessive shunt capacitance to the ground plane, causing a severe local impedance drop (\(Z_0 \approx 30\ \Omega \dots 35\ \Omega\)), return loss degradation, and parasitic insertion loss.

docs.title: Transition Design Criteria:
docs.text:
1. Narrow-Conductor SMA Footprint: The layout incorporates an optimized SMA connector footprint specifically characterized for high-density 4-layer boards, featuring a narrow copper landing pad.

  2. 0603 Component Dimension Matching: The launch trace width from the SMA pin matches the terminal width of adjacent 0603 components (e.g., the TPD1E01B04 TVS diode and 1000 pF AC-coupling capacitor), preventing abrupt step discontinuities along the signal path.

docs.title: 3.5. Via Stitching Shielding and Mechanical Fixturing
3.5.1. Ground Via Stitching Matrix and RF Via Fences
docs.text: To maintain equal ground potential and suppress lateral electromagnetic coupling: * Boundary Via Fencing: All \(50\ \Omega\) CPW-G lines (10 MHz reference input and dual 24 MHz outputs) are flanked on both sides by continuous double-row ground via fences. Via pitch is maintained at \(d \le 2.0\text{ mm}\) (\(\ll \lambda / 20\) at the highest harmonic frequency), forming a localized Faraday cage that bounds electric and magnetic fields. * Board-Wide Via Stitching: A matrix of stitching vias connects the top copper flood (Layer 1), the inner ground plane (Layer 2), and the bottom ground flood (Layer 4). This eliminates floating copper islands, prevents parasitic cavity resonances, and provides low-thermal-resistance dissipation paths for active devices.

docs.title: 3.5.2. Mechanical Mounting Holes
docs.text: To provide structural rigidity and facilitate shielded enclosure assembly: * 4-Corner Mechanical Holes: The PCB incorporates four symmetrical non-plated/plated mounting holes positioned at each corner of the board (sized for standard M3 / M2.5 hardware).

docs.title: 4. Embedded Programming & Supervisory Firmware
docs.text: The STM32G030 supervisory firmware initializes the ADF4002 synthesizer at power-up and immediately enters a quiescent state to eliminate digital noise during RF operation. This section outlines the low-EMI SPI configuration (500 kbit/s, slew-rate-limited drivers), latch transmission sequence, and boot-to-sleep runtime flow.

docs.title: 4.1. Supervisory Control Strategy & EMI Containment Philosophy
docs.text:
The embedded firmware architecture adheres to three core mixed-signal principles:

  1. Deterministic Cold-Start Configuration: The microcontroller's sole operational duty is to configure the Analog Devices ADF4002 frequency synthesizer upon power-up via a dedicated 3-wire Serial Peripheral Interface (SPI). It sequences the 24-bit control words into the internal latches to lock the 24.0 MHz VCXO to the 10.0 MHz reference clock.
  2. Complete Post-Initialization Digital Bus Quiescence: Unlike systems requiring continuous polling or periodic register refresh, the firmware executes ADF4002_Init() exactly once during cold boot. Once transmission completes, all digital communication lines (SCLK, MOSI, LE) remain clamped in static DC logic states. This eliminates digital clock harmonics, substrate switching spikes, and return current transients from coupling into the adjacent analog loop filter, charge pump rail, and VCXO crystal tank.
  3. Controlled Transition Slew Rates (\(dv/dt\) Reduction): High-speed digital edges with sub-nanosecond rise times emit broadband harmonics extending well beyond several hundred megahertz. By intentionally restricting the SPI baud rate and programming the microcontroller's I/O output drivers to low slew rate, radiated and conducted emissions are eliminated at the source.

docs.title: 4.2. Hardware Pinout Allocation & CubeMX Configuration
docs.text:
The STM32G030J6M6 in the SO8N package provides 8 physical pins, offering 6 configurable general-purpose I/O lines. The pin mapping is dedicated strictly to SPI communication, system debugging, and power rails.

Figure 4.1: STM32G030J6M6 8-pin SO8N pin assignment generated in STM32CubeMX.

Pin # Physical Pin Configured Mode Signal Name Target Connection Electrical Function 1 PC14-OSC32_IN (PB8) Alternate Function Push-Pull ADF4002_CLK ADF4002 Pin 1 (CLK) Hardware SPI2 serial shift clock 2 VDD/VDDA Power Supply Rail +3.3V_DIG Clean LDO Digital Rail Microcontroller core & I/O power (\(+3.3\text{ V}\)) 3 VSS/VSSA Ground Reference GND Solid Ground Plane (Layer 2) Common digital ground return 4 NRST System Reset NRST Reset RC Debounce Circuit External hardware reset input 5 PB0 GPIO Output Push-Pull ADF4002_LE ADF4002 Pin 3 (LE) Active-HIGH Latch Enable (Chip Select) 6 PA10 (PA12) Alternate Function Push-Pull ADF4002_MOSI ADF4002 Pin 2 (DATA) Hardware SPI2 serial data output (MSB first) 7 PA13 Alternate Function SYS_SWDIO Programming Header 2-wire Serial Wire Debug (SWD) Data 8 PA14-BOOT0 Alternate Function SYS_SWCLK Programming Header 2-wire Serial Wire Debug (SWD) Clock

The serial link utilizes the integrated hardware SPI2 peripheral, ensuring deterministic transmission timing compliance with the ADF4002 setup and hold specifications (\(t_1, t_2, t_3 \ge 10\text{ ns}\)) without software bit-banging overhead.

docs.title: 4.3.1. Low-Speed SPI Parameter Settings
docs.text:
While the ADF4002 shift register supports serial clock frequencies up to \(20\text{ MHz}\), operating the digital interface at high speeds within a sensitive RF subsystem introduces unnecessary high-frequency noise. The SPI2 peripheral is deliberately throttled to \(500.0\text{ kbit/s}\) via an internal APB clock prescaler.

Figure 4.2: SPI2 parameter settings showing 500 kbit/s baud rate and Mode 0 clock configuration.

  • Frame Format: Motorola standard, 8-bit data size.
  • Bit Orientation: MSB First (most significant bit shifted out first to match the ADF4002 register shift direction).
  • Baud Rate: Set to \(500.0\text{ kbit/s}\) using a prescaler division factor of \(32\) from the internal APB bus clock (\(f_{\text{PCLK}} = 16\text{ MHz}\)).
  • Clock Phase & Polarity: CPOL = Low (\(0\)), CPHA = 1 Edge (\(0\)). Data is set up on MOSI during the clock falling edge and latched into the ADF4002 on the rising edge of SCLK.
  • NSS Management: Software controlled (NSS Signal Type = Software). The Latch Enable line (ADF4002_LE) is driven independently by general-purpose output PB0.

docs.title: 4.3.2. Output Speed Limitation (Maximum Output Speed = Low)
docs.text:
To suppress high-frequency harmonic generation, the output driver slew rates for all active digital lines (ADF4002_MOSI, ADF4002_CLK, and ADF4002_LE) are explicitly restricted to Low (GPIO_SPEED_FREQ_LOW).

Figure 4.3: GPIO Settings in STM32CubeMX demonstrating Maximum Output Speed set to Low.

docs.title: 4.4. ADF4002 Latch Architecture & Register Mapping
docs.text:
The ADF4002 frequency synthesizer integrates a 24-bit shift register. Data is transferred serially on each rising edge of CLK. When LE transitions from LOW to HIGH, the data stored in the shift register is loaded into the internal latch addressed by the two lowest control bits [C2, C1] (DB1, DB0).

Figure 4.4: Latch summary and bit allocation extracted from the ADF4002 datasheet.

The device incorporates four functional 24-bit latches: * Reference Counter Latch (C2=0, C1=0): Sets the 14-bit R divider (\(R = 5\)), anti-backlash pulse width (\(1.3\text{ ns}\)), and Lock Detect Precision. * N Counter Latch (C2=0, C1=1): Sets the 13-bit N divider (\(N = 12\)) and prescaler control. * Function Latch (C2=1, C1=0): Configures charge pump current (\(I_{\text{CP}} = 5.0\text{ mA}\), Code 7 with \(R_{\text{SET}} = 5.1\text{ k}\Omega\)), Phase Detector polarity (Positive for non-inverting loop filter), and MUXOUT mode (Digital Lock Detect). * Initialization Latch (C2=1, C1=1): Functional mirror of the Function Latch used to reset internal counters and establish deterministic states upon cold start.

docs.title: 4.5. Firmware Architecture, Execution Flow & Repository Implementation
4.5.1. Synthesizer Initialization Sequence (ADF4002_Init)
docs.text:
The initialization routine configures the ADF4002 via a deterministic 4-stage pipeline, strictly following the manufacturer-specified power-on sequence:

[ Power-On Delay ] ──► [ Bitfield Construction ] ──► [ Sequential SPI Latch Dispatch ] ──► [ Return HAL_OK ]
     (100 ms)                 (4 x 24-bit words)          (Init ──► Func ──► R ──► N)          (Sleep / Idle)

  1. Power Stabilization Delay (100 ms): Executes a blocking startup delay (HAL_Delay(100U)) immediately upon entry to guarantee that LDO analog/digital rails (\(+3.3\text{V}_{\text{ANA}}\), \(+3.3\text{V}_{\text{DIG}}\)) and the VCXO crystal reach stable steady-state DC levels before communication starts.

  2. Control Word Construction: Packs the operating parameters into four 24-bit frame buffers with designated latch address bits [C2, C1]:

  3. Initialization Latch (0x...3): Forces an internal counter reset, disables outputs, and sets PFD polarity.
  4. Function Latch (0x...2): Releases counter resets, programs charge pump drive current (\(I_{\text{CP}}\) mapped simultaneously to both Settings 1 and 2), and routes Lock Detect to MUXOUT.
  5. Reference (R) Counter Latch (0x...0): Loads division ratio \(R = 5\) to establish \(f_{\text{PFD}} = 2.0\text{ MHz}\).

  6. Feedback (N) Counter Latch (0x...1): Loads division ratio \(N = 12\) (\(24.0\text{ MHz} \to 2.0\text{ MHz}\)) with CP Gain = 0, activating closed-loop phase comparison.

  7. Sequential Transmission & Fail-Safe Latching: Iterates through an atomic loop (words[0] to words[3]):

  8. Dispatches each 24-bit word serially via ADF4002_Write24() over SPI2 at 500 kbit/s.
  9. Fail-Safe Mechanism: If any frame transfer fails (HAL_ERROR or timeout), the function immediately aborts and returns the error code without pulsing LE on subsequent latches.
  10. On completion of all 4 latches, returns HAL_OK and yields the MCU to an idle state (__WFI()).

docs.title: 4.5.2. Firmware Source Repository
docs.text:
The complete low-level driver implementation, register bitmasks, and initialization routines are version-controlled in the project repository:

  • Synthesizer Driver Header (adf4002.h): https://github.com/tuchau1404/solar_correlator/blob/main/firmware/10_24MHz_PLL/Core/Inc/adf4002.h Contains configuration macros, divider constants (\(R=5, N=12\)), charge pump codes, and function prototypes.

  • Synthesizer Driver Implementation (adf4002.c): https://github.com/tuchau1404/solar_correlator/blob/main/firmware/10_24MHz_PLL/Core/Src/adf4002.c Implements 24-bit word construction, byte-packing, low-speed SPI transmission, and LE latch pulse timing.

docs.title: 5. Laboratory Verification & Test Procedures
docs.text: This section details the empirical validation and bench characterization of the assembled Dual-Channel 24 MHz PLL Clock Distribution board. Measurements were conducted under nominal laboratory conditions (\(T_{\text{amb}} = 25^\circ\text{C}\)) to confirm DC operating points, reference signal conditioning, time-domain waveform integrity, harmonic rejection, and frequency accuracy against design targets.

docs.title: 5.1. Testbench Setup & Instrumentation Matrix
docs.text:
The Device Under Test (DUT) was integrated into a multi-instrument RF verification testbench. All frequency-sensitive instruments were locked to a common \(10.000000\text{ MHz}\) GPS-Disciplined Oscillator (GPSDO) master timebase to eliminate measurement reference drift.

Figure 5.1: Full laboratory verification bench showing the DC supply, 10 MHz reference source, oscilloscope, spectrum analyzer, and precision frequency counter connected to the DUT.

Equipment Type Model / Instrument Measurement Role Configuration / Settings DC Power Supply Keysight E3631A / Rigol DP832 Main DC power feed \(+5.00\text{ V}_{\text{DC}}\), current limit set to \(250\text{ mA}\) Reference Source BG7TBL GPSDO / SDG2042X Master 10.0 MHz reference \(10.000\text{ MHz}\) sine wave, \(+7.0\text{ dBm}\) into \(50\ \Omega\) Digital Storage Scope Keysight DSOX3054T (\(500\text{ MHz}\), \(5\text{ GSa/s}\)) Time-domain waveform & slicer check Channel 1 & 2 set to \(50\ \Omega\) DC coupling Spectrum Analyzer Rohde & Schwarz FSC3 (\(9\text{ kHz} \dots 3\text{ GHz}\)) Harmonic suppression & spur analysis \(\text{RBW} = 10\text{ kHz}\), \(\text{VBW} = 10\text{ kHz}\), Span \(= 120\text{ MHz}\) Frequency Counter Keysight 53220A (\(350\text{ MHz}\), 12 digits/s) Carrier accuracy & Allan deviation 1 s gate time, external \(10\text{ MHz}\) GPSDO reference RF Coaxial Loads Huber+Suhner \(50\ \Omega\) SMA Terminations Port impedance balancing Return loss \(S_{11} < -35\text{ dB}\) up to \(2\text{ GHz}\)

docs.title: 5.2. DC Power Rail & Current Consumption Verification
docs.text:
The board was energized via the screw terminal (\(+5.0\text{V}_{\text{IN}}\)). Regulated output rails and total supply currents were verified using a digital multimeter before and after synthesizer latch programming:

Figure 5.2: Precision current monitor displaying total DUT current consumption in locked steady state.

  • Supply Rails:
  • \(+3.3\text{V}_{\text{ANA}}\) (LDO 1): Measured \(3.302\text{V}\) (ripple \(< 10\ \mu\text{V}_{\text{RMS}}\)).
  • \(+3.3\text{V}_{\text{DIG}}\) (LDO 2): Measured \(3.298\text{V}\).
  • Tuning Voltage (\(V_{\text{tune}}\)): Settled stably at \(1.68\text{V}\) at lock (optimal center of the \(0.3\text{V} \dots 3.0\text{V}\) tuning window).
  • Current Consumption Profile:
  • Free-Running / Unlocked (Boot): \(I_{\text{DD}} \approx 42\text{ mA}\).
  • Phase-Locked Steady State (MCU Asleep via __WFI): Measured \(58.4\text{ mA}\) (\(P_{\text{DC}} \approx 292\text{ mW}\)). This confirms low thermal dissipation across the compact enclosure.

docs.title: 5.3. 10 MHz Reference Input Slicer Check (Sine-to-Square)
docs.text:
The self-biased 74LVC1G04 inverter slicer stage was probed to verify conversion of the external GPSDO sine wave into a steep CMOS edge matching the ADF4002 input boundary (\(\text{SR} > 50\text{ V/}\mu\text{s}\)).

Figure 5.3: Dual-channel oscilloscope capture showing input 10 MHz sine wave (Ch1, yellow) and sliced 3.3V CMOS square wave at ADF4002 REFIN (Ch2, blue).

  • Input Waveform (Ch1 — Yellow): \(10.000\text{ MHz}\) sine wave, \(V_{\text{pp}} = 1.41\text{ V}_{\text{pp}}\) (\(+7.0\text{ dBm}\) into \(50\ \Omega\)). Zero-crossing slew rate: \(\approx 44.3\text{ V/}\mu\text{s}\) (insufficient without slicing).
  • Sliced Output at REFIN (Ch2 — Blue):
  • Symmetrical square wave swinging rail-to-rail (\(0.0\text{V} \dots 3.3\text{V}\)).
  • Measured rise time (\(10\% \dots 90\%\)): \(t_r = 1.82\text{ ns}\).
  • Extracted Transition Slew Rate: $\(\text{SR}_{\text{measured}} \approx \frac{0.8 \times 3.3\text{V}}{1.82\text{ ns}} \approx \mathbf{1450\text{ V/}\mu\text{s}} \quad (\mathbf{1.45\text{ V/ns}})\)$
  • Duty Cycle: \(49.8\% / 50.2\%\), ensuring zero even-order harmonic degradation. The slew rate exceeds the \(50\text{ V/}\mu\text{s}\) specification by \(> 28\times\).

docs.title: 5.4. Time-Domain Output Characterization (24 MHz Sinusoid)
docs.text:
Both RF output channels (OUT 1 and OUT 2) were terminated into active \(50\ \Omega\) oscilloscope channels through matched coaxial cables to evaluate amplitude, waveform symmetry, and transient damping.

Figure 5.4: Oscilloscope capture of the 24.0 MHz sinusoidal outputs on OUT 1 and OUT 2 terminated into 50 Ω.

  • Peak-to-Peak Amplitude: \(V_{\text{pp}} = \mathbf{1.04\text{ V}_{\text{pp}}}\) (\(0.368\text{ V}_{\text{RMS}}\), equivalent to \(+4.32\text{ dBm}\) into \(50\ \Omega\)), fully compliant with the target \(+4.0 \dots +5.0\text{ dBm}\) drive window.
  • Waveform Purity: Zero visible ringing, plateau clipping, or overshoot due to the return loss improvement provided by the \(6\text{ dB}\) \(\pi\)-pad attenuator.
  • Channel-to-Channel Skew (\(\Delta t\)): Static propagation delay difference between OUT 1 and OUT 2 measured \(< 42\text{ ps}\), well within the backend calibration window.

docs.title: 5.5. Frequency-Domain Characterization (Harmonics & PFD Spurs)
docs.text:
Spectral purity, harmonic roll-off, and charge pump spur suppression were characterized using the R&S FSC3 Spectrum Analyzer connected to OUT 1 (with OUT 2 terminated into \(50\ \Omega\)).

Figure 5.5: RF spectrum scan from 10 MHz to 130 MHz showing the fundamental 24 MHz carrier and suppression of 2nd and 3rd harmonics.

  • Fundamental Carrier (\(f_0 = 24.000\text{ MHz}\)): Delivered power measured at \(+4.28\text{ dBm}\).
  • 2nd Harmonic (\(2f_0 = 48.000\text{ MHz}\)): Suppressed to \(-51.6\text{ dBc}\) (attenuated by symmetrical CMOS buffer switching).
  • 3rd Harmonic (\(3f_0 = 72.000\text{ MHz}\)): Suppressed to \(-46.2\text{ dBc}\), exceeding the system requirement (\(\le -40.0\text{ dBc}\)) by \(6.2\text{ dB}\) through the 5th-order Butterworth low-pass filter.
  • PFD Reference Spurs (\(f_0 \pm 2.0\text{ MHz}\)): Residual spur levels at \(22.0\text{ MHz}\) and \(26.0\text{ MHz}\) remain below \(-86.0\text{ dBc}\), confirming the out-of-band rejection of the 3rd-order loop filter.

docs.title: 5.6. Frequency Accuracy & Long-Term Stability (Time Counter)
docs.text:
Absolute carrier frequency, gate repeatability, and tracking stability were measured using the Keysight 53220A Frequency Counter locked to the external GPSDO master reference.

Figure 5.6: Frequency counter readout showing carrier lock at exactly 24.000 000 0 MHz over a 1-second continuous gate window.

  • Measured Carrier Frequency: \(24.000\,000\,02\text{ MHz}\) (mean over 1000 continuous samples).
  • Carrier Frequency Offset: \(\Delta f \approx +0.02\text{ Hz}\) (fractional offset \(< 1.0 \times 10^{-9}\)), limited strictly by the reference GPSDO timebase accuracy.
  • Standard Deviation (\(\sigma_f\) @ 1 s gate): \(\sigma_f = 14.8\text{ mHz}\), verifying zero cycle slipping and deterministic lock stability over long observation intervals.

docs.title: 1. System Context & Physical Problem Formulation in Radio Interferometry
1.1. Overview and System Architecture
docs.text:
In a dual-channel decametric radio interferometer operating across the \(30.0\text{--}40.0\text{ MHz}\) frequency band, two independent Software-Defined Radio (SDR) receivers (SDRplay RSPdx) act as spatial sensing nodes. To detect and characterize transient solar radio emissions (such as Type II and Type III solar bursts) and resolve their spatial-temporal dynamics, the system processes raw digitized baseband signals using a distributed FX correlator architecture hosted on an embedded platform (Raspberry Pi 5).

Although both SDR receivers are disciplined by a shared external \(24.0\text{ MHz}\) reference clock fed into their respective REFin ports to ensure strictly identical analog-to-digital conversion sampling frequencies (\(f_{s1} = f_{s2} = 10.0\text{ MSPS}\)), hardware-level clock synchronization alone does not resolve startup time offsets, internal analog phase dispersions, or dynamic gain drifts. An internal broadband avalanche noise source serves as an in-situ hardware calibration standard, providing the entropy and radiometric reference required to address four core physical and digital signal processing challenges prior to celestial observation.

docs.title: 1.2. USB Startup Sample Delay Alignment (k_offset — Module 2)
1.2.1. Root Cause of Startup Misalignment
docs.text:
Operating system constraints dictate that the proprietary SDR hardware driver API (sdrplay_api v3) permits only a single active receiver instance per OS process. Consequently, a multi-process architecture is deployed wherein the parent process spawns two dedicated producer processes via fork(). Each child process independently issues sdrplay_api_Open(), executes hardware selection, and negotiates stream initializations via sdrplay_api_Init().

Even though the underlying ADC samplers advance on the identical \(24.0\text{ MHz}\) clock edges, the operational startup times of the two data streams are non-deterministic. Variations in Linux kernel thread scheduling, USB host controller interrupt latency, device enumeration timings, and internal decimation filter flushing introduce an arbitrary delay:

\[ \Delta t_\text{startup} \in [10\text{ ms}, 50\text{ ms}] \]

At a baseband sampling rate of \(f_s = 10\text{ MSPS}\) (corresponding to a sample period of \(T_s = 100\text{ ns}\)), a temporal startup discrepancy of merely \(30\text{ ms}\) yields an initial sample index offset of:

\[ k_\text{offset} = \Delta t_\text{startup} \cdot f_s \approx 300,000\text{ samples} \]

docs.title: 1.2.2. Theoretical Necessity of Coarse Sample Synchronization
docs.text:
The complex cross-correlation function between the baseband analytical sequences \(x_1[n]\) and \(x_2[n]\) across a discrete lag parameter \(k\) is defined as:

\[ R_{12}[k] = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} x_1[n] \cdot x_2^*[n - k] \]

In the correlator pipeline, spectral decomposition (the F-Engine) processes finite snapshot blocks of length \(N = 2048\) (or \(N = 65,536\) during calibration). If an uncompensated integer offset \(k_\text{offset} \neq 0\) persists such that \(|k_\text{offset}| \ge N\), the block extracted from Channel 1 represents an electromagnetic epoch that shares no temporal overlap with the block extracted from Channel 2. Under this condition:

\[ \mathbb{E}\{x_1[n] \cdot x_2^*[n - k_\text{offset}]\} = 0 \]

The cross-power expectation collapses entirely into uncorrelated baseline noise, completely extinguishing interferometric fringe formation. Therefore, coarse synchronization must deterministically align the two data queues to within \(|k_\text{residual}| \le 1\text{ sample}\) (\(100\text{ ns}\)) before downstream cross-multiplication.

docs.title: 1.2.3. Broadband Gaussian Noise vs. Continuous-Wave (CW) Signals
1.4. Absolute Flux Scaling & Semiconductor Thermal Drift
1.4.1. The Need for Absolute Radiometric Flux Calibration
1.4.2. Semiconductor Physics of Thermal Gain Degradation
docs.text:
During continuous decametric observation runs at \(10\text{ MSPS}\), the active digital baseband processing and internal LNA/mixer circuitry dissipate sustained electrical power. Within the shielded die-cast aluminum enclosure of the RSPdx, internal board temperatures rise from ambient room temperature (\(25^\circ\text{C}\)) to a thermal equilibrium plateau between \(50^\circ\text{C}\) and \(60^\circ\text{C}\).

In active silicon bipolar and field-effect transistors, the thermal voltage is governed by:

\[ V_T = \frac{k_B T}{q} \]

where \(k_B\) is the Boltzmann constant, \(q\) is the elementary charge, and \(T\) is absolute temperature in Kelvin. As temperature increases: 1. Carrier Mobility Reduction: Increased phonon scattering diminishes charge carrier mobility \(\mu(T) \propto T^{-3/2}\), degrading the small-signal transconductance:

\[ g_m \approx \sqrt{2\mu C_{ox} \frac{W}{L} I_D} \]
  1. Gain Drift: The open-loop voltage gain of front-end Low-Noise Amplifiers (LNAs) and Programmable Gain Amplifiers (PGAs) drops proportionally (\(G \propto g_m \cdot R_L\)), manifesting as continuous thermal gain drift (\(\approx -0.01\text{ to } -0.03\text{ dB/}^\circ\text{C}\)).

docs.title: 1.4.3. Inter-Receiver Gain Asymmetry and Cross-Correlation Distortion
docs.text:
Because the two RSPdx units are distinct physical enclosures with independent PCB assemblies, component-level manufacturing variations and subtle differences in localized convective cooling cause them to reach unequal equilibrium temperatures:

\[ T_{\text{SDR}_1} \neq T_{\text{SDR}_2} \implies G_1(t, T) \neq G_2(t, T) \]

The magnitude of the interferometric cross-power spectrum is proportional to the geometric mean of the channel gains:

\[ |S_{12}(f)| = \sqrt{G_1(f) \cdot G_2(f)} \cdot |S_\text{sky}(f)| \]

If Receiver 1 experiences a gain compression of \(-0.6\text{ dB}\) while Receiver 2 experiences \(-1.4\text{ dB}\) due to unequal thermal stabilization, the cross-correlation amplitude will drift dynamically over time. Absent dynamic baseline gain compensation, observers cannot distinguish whether a fluctuating signal amplitude corresponds to an authentic solar burst event or an instrumental thermal artifact.

docs.title: 1.5. The Broadband Noise Standard: In-Situ Solution and Thermal Compensation
1.5.1. Avalanche Mechanism & Fixed Excess Noise Ratio (ENR)
1.5.3. Resolving Calibration Drift: Pulsed Gating vs. Continuous Receiver Dissipation
docs.text:
A critical engineering consideration is whether the calibration noise source itself suffers from thermal drift. While semiconductor avalanche noise does exhibit a minor positive temperature coefficient (\(\approx +2\text{ to } +5\text{ mV/}^\circ\text{C}\) on \(V_\text{BR}\), translating to an output power drift of \(\approx -0.015\text{ dB/}^\circ\text{C}\)), the operational duty cycles of the SDRs and the noise standard prevent systemic calibration errors:

  1. Continuous Operation of SDRs: The RSPdx receivers and host USB pipelines operate continuously 24 hours a day to capture stochastic solar flares, remaining in a steady-state thermal regime (\(50^\circ\text{C}\text{--}60^\circ\text{C}\)) where internal gain drift is persistent.
  2. Pulsed Operation of the Noise Source: The avalanche noise source is not powered continuously. Instead, it is gated via an isolated GPIO line on the Raspberry Pi 5. The source is energized only during dedicated calibration sweeps lasting \(300\text{ ms} \text{ to } 1000\text{ ms}\) at periodic intervals (e.g., once every 30 minutes or prior to observation runs), resulting in a duty cycle of:
\[ \text{Duty Cycle} = \frac{\tau_\text{on}}{\tau_\text{period}} \le \frac{1.0\text{ s}}{1800\text{ s}} \approx 0.056\% \]
  1. Suppression of Self-Heating: With an operational duty cycle well below \(0.1\%\), the 2N2222 transistor die experiences zero internal self-heating (\(\Delta T_\text{junction} \approx 0\)). The circuit operates at ambient chassis temperature throughout the measurement pulse, preserving the absolute stability of the physical ENR value.

Furthermore, because the broadband noise signal is split symmetrically into both receiver channels via a 1:2 Wilkinson divider located in immediate physical proximity to the tuners, any common-mode phase or amplitude perturbations introduced by the calibration circuit affect both receivers equally, naturally canceling out in the differential phase matrix:

\[ \Delta\phi_\text{noise} = \arg(S_{12}) = \phi_\text{noise}(t) - \phi_\text{noise}(t) = 0^\circ \]

This ensures that the hardware standard delivers an invariant zero-phase and fixed-power benchmark across the lifespan of the instrument.

docs.title: 3.1. LOG ENTRY #01: Bench Characterization of BJT 2N2222 Breakdown
3.1.1. Objective and Measurement Specifications
docs.text:
• Primary Objective: Determine the precise reverse avalanche breakdown voltage (\(V_{\text{BR}}\)), dynamic junction resistance (\(r_d\)), and optimal noise-generation current of the through-hole (TO-92) NPN 2N2222 Base–Emitter (B-E) junction across the \(30.0 - 40.0\text{ MHz}\) IF passband.

  • Instrumentation & Test Equipment:

  • Precision Source-Measure Unit (SMU): Chroma 58221-200-2 (Configured in 4-Wire Constant Current [CC] mode; voltage compliance set to \(15.0\text{ V}\)).
  • RF Spectrum Analyzer: Rohde & Schwarz CMU200 (Selected receiver port: RF4 IN / High Sensitivity, input impedance \(50\ \Omega\)).

  • Coupling & Matching Components: \(1.0\text{ nF}\) high-Q ceramic disc DC-blocking capacitor (\(50\text{ V}\) rating, \(X_C \approx 4.5\ \Omega\) at \(35\text{ MHz}\)); calibrated \(10.0\text{ dB}\) coaxial \(\Pi\)-network attenuator (\(50\ \Omega\), DC–3 GHz, \(\text{VSWR} < 1.15\)).

  • Analyzer Instrument Setup:

  • Center Frequency (\(f_c\)): \(35.0\text{ MHz}\)
  • Frequency Span (\(\Delta f\)): \(10.0\text{ MHz}\) (sweep interval: \(30.0\text{ MHz} - 40.0\text{ MHz}\))

  • Resolution Bandwidth (RBW): \(1.0\text{ MHz}\)

  • Detector Mode: RMS / Power Average (linear power averaging across 20 consecutive traces to stabilize stochastic microplasma power fluctuations)

docs.title: 3.1.2.2. Excess Noise Ratio (ENR) Calculation
docs.text:
Excess Noise Ratio (ENR) defines the generated noise power spectral density relative to the Johnson–Nyquist thermal noise floor of a matched load at standard reference temperature (\(T_0 = 290\text{ K}\)):

\[ \text{ENR} = 10 \log_{10} \left( \frac{T_{\text{hot}} - T_0}{T_0} \right) = 10 \log_{10} \left( \frac{P_{\text{PSD}} - P_{0/\text{Hz}}}{P_{0/\text{Hz}}} \right) \]

At \(T_0 = 290\text{ K}\), the baseline thermal noise density is:

\[ P_{0/\text{Hz}} = k T_0 = -174.0\text{ dBm/Hz} \]

When measuring on an analyzer configured with a resolution bandwidth of \(\text{RBW} = 1.0\text{ MHz} = 10^6\text{ Hz}\), the baseline thermal noise floor within that filter window expands by:

\[ 10 \log_{10}(10^6) = +60.0\text{ dB} \] \[ P_{\text{floor, 1MHz}} = -174.0\text{ dBm/Hz} + 60.0\text{ dB} = -114.0\text{ dBm} \]

For a detected power level \(P_{\text{meas}}\) (in \(\text{dBm}\)) measured by the CMU200 at the output of the \(10\text{ dB}\) attenuator pad:

\[ \text{ENR}_{\text{sys}}\ (\text{dB}) = P_{\text{meas}}\ (\text{dBm}) - (-114.0\text{ dBm}) = P_{\text{meas}} + 114.0 \]

Accounting for the insertion loss of the matching attenuator (\(A_{\text{pad}} = 10.0\text{ dB}\)), the intrinsic raw ENR generated directly across the BJT junction (\(\text{ENR}_{\text{DUT}}\)) is:

\[ \text{ENR}_{\text{DUT}}\ (\text{dB}) = \text{ENR}_{\text{sys}} + A_{\text{pad}} = P_{\text{meas}} + 124.0 \]

The total integrated power delivered over the entire \(10.0\text{ MHz}\) receiver passband (\(B = 10\text{ MHz}\)) is:

\[ P_{\text{total, 10MHz}} = P_{\text{meas}} + 10 \log_{10} \left( \frac{10\text{ MHz}}{1\text{ MHz}} \right) = P_{\text{meas}} + 10.0\text{ dB} \]

docs.title: 3.1.6. Engineering Conclusions & Design Next Steps
docs.text:
1. Operating Point Selection:

  2. The optimal bias current is locked at \(I_{\text{bias}} = 2.0\text{ mA}\) (\(V_{\text{BR}} = 9.21\text{ V}\)). At this operating point, the avalanche core produces an intrinsic raw ENR of \(+44.0\text{ dB}\) (equivalent to \(-70.0\text{ dBm}\) integrated over the entire \(10\text{ MHz}\) receiver passband) with optimum spectral flatness (\(\pm 0.35\text{ dB}\) across \(30.0 - 40.0\text{ MHz}\)).

  3. Gain Budgeting for Receiver Front-End:

  4. The SDRplay RSPdx receiver front-end operating at nominal gain settings (GAIN_GRDB = 30) requires an injected input level of \(-55.0\text{ dBm}\) to \(-45.0\text{ dBm}\) to guarantee a cross-correlation Peak-to-Noise Ratio (\(\text{PNR}\)) exceeding \(30\text{ dB}\).

  5. Because the post-attenuator power from the raw core at \(2.0\text{ mA}\) is only \(-80.0\text{ dBm}\) (over \(10\text{ MHz}\)), an intermediate RF buffer stage (\(Q_2\)) delivering \(+25.0\text{ dB}\) to \(+30.0\text{ dB}\) of linear power gain is mandatory prior to the final \(50\ \Omega\) matching network.

docs.title: 3.2. LOG ENTRY #02: Discrete Active Current Source Implementation (2-BJT PNP)
3.2.1. Problem Statement & Quantitative Error Analysis
docs.text:
Bench laboratory programmable DC supplies (such as the Chroma source) cannot be integrated onto the final embedded receiver shield in the field. An initial passive pull-up resistor topology powered from an unregulated or semi-regulated \(+15\text{ V}\) DC supply rail leaves an extremely narrow operating voltage headroom:

\[ \Delta V = V_{\text{CC}} - V_{\text{BR}} = 15\text{ V} - 9.2\text{ V} = 5.8\text{ V} \]

To establish the target nominal avalanche bias current \(I_{\text{bias}} = 2.0\text{ mA}\), the required passive pull-up resistance is:

\[ R_{\text{pull-up}} = \frac{\Delta V}{I_{\text{bias}}} = \frac{5.8\text{ V}}{2.0\text{ mA}} = 2.9\text{ k}\Omega \]

Because a purely passive pull-up topology provides zero active negative feedback or power supply rejection (PSRR), any line noise, switching ripple, or DC bus fluctuations directly perturb the reverse-biased junction breakdown point:

  • Switching Power Supply Ripple (\(\Delta V_{\text{ripple}} = 100\text{ mV}_{\text{p-p}}\)): High-frequency ripple from step-up/step-down converters produces direct instantaneous current modulation:
\[ \Delta I_{\text{ripple}} = \frac{100\text{ mV}}{2.9\text{ k}\Omega} \approx 0.0345\text{ mA} \quad (\approx 1.72\%) \]

This periodic variation amplitude-modulates (AM) the avalanche plasma carrier density, generating spurious spectral spurs across the RF passband and destroying the Gaussian white-noise characteristics of the source.

  • DC Voltage Drift (\(\Delta V_{\text{drift}} = 500\text{ mV}\) drop): A minor line droop of \(500\text{ mV}\) (representing a \(3.33\%\) drop on a nominal \(15\text{ V}\) rail) induces a severe static current collapse:
\[ \Delta I_{\text{drift}} = \frac{0.5\text{ V}}{2.9\text{ k}\Omega} \approx 0.172\text{ mA} \quad (\approx \mathbf{8.62\%}) \]
  • Impact on Excess Noise Ratio (ENR): In the avalanche breakdown region, the generated shot and microplasma spectral noise power density is directly proportional to the DC bias current (\(\overline{i_n^2} \propto I_{\text{bias}}\)). Consequently, an \(8.62\%\) current drop directly alters the Excess Noise Ratio (ENR):
\[ \Delta \text{ENR} \approx 10 \log_{10}\left(1 + \frac{\Delta I}{I_{\text{bias}}}\right) = 10 \log_{10}(1 - 0.0862) \approx \mathbf{-0.39\text{ dB}} \]

In radio astronomy calibration budgets, where the maximum permissible uncertainty is typically constrained within \(\pm 0.15\text{ dB}\), an ENR error of \(-0.39\text{ dB}\) skews radiometric system temperature (\(T_{\text{sys}}\)) and sky flux density calculations by approximately \(8.6\%\). This necessitated the design of an active, high-PSRR constant current source.

docs.title: 3.2.2. Circuit Architecture
docs.text:
To insulate the avalanche breakdown junction from supply line fluctuations, an active, discrete two-transistor constant current source was designed using two matched PNP BJTs (2N2907, designated \(Q_{\text{pass}}\) and \(Q_{\text{sense}}\)).

Figure 1: Schematic diagram of the discrete 2-BJT PNP active current source delivering regulated bias to the avalanche junction.

docs.title: 3.2.2.1. Feedback Regulation Mechanism
docs.text:
1. The load current flowing into the avalanche breakdown diode passes entirely through the sense resistor \(R_{\text{sense}}\) positioned at the emitter of the series-pass transistor \(Q_{\text{pass}}\).
  2. As the output current rises, the voltage drop across \(R_{\text{sense}}\) increases:
\[ V_{\text{sense}} = I_{\text{bias}} \cdot R_{\text{sense}} \]
  1. This voltage directly biases the Base-Emitter junction of the sensing transistor \(Q_{\text{sense}}\). When \(V_{\text{sense}}\) reaches the threshold \(V_{\text{BE(on)}} \approx 0.65\text{ V}\), \(Q_{\text{sense}}\) begins conducting collector current.
  2. The collector of \(Q_{\text{sense}}\) pulls the Base node of \(Q_{\text{pass}}\) upward toward \(V_{\text{CC}}\), reducing the \(V_{\text{EB}}\) drive of \(Q_{\text{pass}}\) and throttling back conduction.
  3. This negative feedback loop clamps \(I_{\text{bias}}\) to a stable constant value, providing dynamic output impedance in the megaohm range and effectively attenuating ripple on \(V_{\text{CC}}\).

docs.title: 3.2.3.1. Current Sense Resistor (R_sense)
docs.text:
The nominal sensing resistance is calculated using the forward-bias threshold of \(Q_{\text{sense}}\):

\[ R_{\text{sense}} = \frac{V_{\text{BE(sense)}}}{I_{\text{bias}}} \approx \frac{0.65\text{ V}}{2.0\text{ mA}} \approx 325\ \Omega \]
  • Selected Nominal Value: The closest standard E24 resistor is \(R_{\text{nominal}} = 330\ \Omega\).

docs.title: 3.2.3.2. Base Pull-Down Resistor (R_pull)
docs.text:
A pull-down resistor \(R_{\text{pull}} = 10\text{ k}\Omega\) ties the Base of \(Q_{\text{pass}}\) to ground (GND), ensuring adequate base current to saturate or drive \(Q_{\text{pass}}\) into its linear forward-active operating region across variations:

\[ V_{\text{EC(pass)}} = V_{\text{CC}} - V_{\text{sense}} - V_{\text{BR}} = 15\text{ V} - 0.65\text{ V} - 9.2\text{ V} = 5.15\text{ V} \gg V_{\text{EC(sat)}} \]

With \(V_{\text{EC(pass)}} \approx 5.15\text{ V}\), the transistor operates deep within its active region, ensuring high output resistance (\(r_o\)) and preventing early-voltage clipping.

docs.title: 3.2.4. Hardware Implementation & Lab Bench Setup
docs.text:
The circuit was prototyped on a low-parasitic copper clad board for zero-baseline laboratory validation prior to PCB integration.

Figure 2: Laboratory bench test setup showing the breadboard prototype of the 2-BJT current source driving the avalanche diode, monitored via digital multimeter and spectrum analyzer.

docs.title: 3.2.6. Line Regulation & Dynamic Output Impedance
docs.text:
• Line Regulation Sensitivity (\(S_I\)): Over the full \(\Delta V_{\text{source}} = 2.0\text{ V}\) span, \(V_{\text{EB}}\) remains tightly clamped at \(0.62\text{ V}\) with a single-digit measurement fluctuation bounded within \(\Delta V_{\text{EB}} \le 0.01\text{ V}\) (\(10\text{ mV}\), matching instrument resolution). The resulting maximum bias drift is:
\[ \Delta I_{\text{bias}} = 1.879\text{ mA} - 1.848\text{ mA} \approx 0.0303\text{ mA} \quad (30.3\ \mu\text{A}) \] \[ S_{I} = \frac{\Delta I_{\text{bias}}}{\Delta V_{\text{source}}} = \frac{0.0303\text{ mA}}{2.0\text{ V}} \approx 0.0152\text{ mA/V} = 15.15\ \mu\text{A/V} \]

Expressed as relative sensitivity:

\[ \frac{\Delta I_{\text{bias}} / I_{\text{bias}}}{\Delta V_{\text{source}}} = \frac{1.61\%}{2.0\text{ V}} \approx 0.81\%/\text{V} \]
  • Dynamic Output Resistance (\(r_{\text{out}}\)): The small-signal dynamic impedance looking into the collector of the active pass transistor \(Q_{\text{pass}}\) is:
\[ r_{\text{out}} = \frac{\Delta V_{\text{source}}}{\Delta I_{\text{bias}}} = \frac{2.0\text{ V}}{30.3\ \mu\text{A}} \approx 66.0\text{ k}\Omega \]

Compared to a passive pull-up resistor (\(R_{\text{passive}} = \frac{15.0\text{ V} - 9.27\text{ V}}{2.0\text{ mA}} \approx 2.87\text{ k}\Omega\)), the active circuit increases dynamic source impedance by:

\[ \frac{r_{\text{out}}}{R_{\text{passive}}} = \frac{66.0\text{ k}\Omega}{2.87\text{ k}\Omega} \approx 23.0\times \quad (\mathbf{+27.2\text{ dB}}\text{ PSRR improvement}) \]
  • Base Current Divergence Analysis: While \(I_{\text{bias}}\) remains constant at \(1.88\text{ mA}\), the measured total current \(I_{\text{source}}\) increases from \(3.13\text{ mA}\) to \(3.34\text{ mA}\) (\(\Delta I_{\text{source}} = 0.21\text{ mA}\)). This perfectly correlates with the static current drawn by the base pull-down resistor \(R_{\text{pull}} = 10\text{ k}\Omega\) connected to ground:
\[ \Delta I_{\text{pull}} = \frac{\Delta V_{\text{pass,B}}}{R_{\text{pull}}} = \frac{14.75\text{ V} - 12.75\text{ V}}{10\text{ k}\Omega} = \frac{2.00\text{ V}}{10\text{ k}\Omega} = 0.20\text{ mA} \]

This confirms that excess line voltage is entirely dissipated across the passive biasing branch, while the core avalanche junction is decoupled and fed by a constant current.

docs.title: 3.3. LOG ENTRY #03: MMIC Buffer Amplifier (GALI-74) & Thermal Optimization of R_bias
docs.text:
• Power Budget Target: Deliver \(-40\text{ dBm}\) total power across the \(10\text{ MHz}\) bandwidth (\(30 - 40\text{ MHz}\)) to drive the RSPdx receivers at \(-14\text{ dBFS} \dots -18\text{ dBFS}\) without ADC clipping. On the CMU200 with \(\text{RBW} = 1\text{ MHz}\), this corresponds to: $\(P_{\text{RBW}} = -40\text{ dBm} - 10\log_{10}\left(\frac{10\text{ MHz}}{1\text{ MHz}}\right) = -50\text{ dBm}\)$

  • MMIC Operating Point: Mini-Circuits GALI-74 requires a device operating current \(I_d \approx 80\text{ mA}\) at device voltage \(V_d \approx 4.8\text{ V}\).

  • Bias Resistance Calculation (from 15V Supply): $\(R_{\text{bias}} = \frac{V_{\text{CC}} - V_d}{I_d} = \frac{15.0\text{ V} - 4.8\text{ V}}{0.080\text{ A}} = \frac{10.2\text{ V}}{0.080\text{ A}} = 127.5\ \Omega\)$

    \[P_{\text{diss}} = I_d^2 \cdot R_{\text{bias}} = (0.08\text{ A})^2 \times 127.5\ \Omega \approx 0.816\text{ W} \approx 0.82\text{ W}\]

  • Engineering Trade-off & Cost Optimization:

    • Issue: A dedicated \(127\ \Omega\), \(>1\text{ W}\) precision resistor (2512 SMD or TO-220) is expensive and difficult to source locally.
    • Implementation: Paralleled four \(510\ \Omega\) SMD 1206 resistors (standard E24 series):
      • Equivalent Resistance: \(R_{\text{total}} = \frac{510\ \Omega}{4} = 127.5\ \Omega\) (\(0.0\%\) error against target).
      • Power Capability: Rated at \(0.25\text{ W}\) each, four 1206 packages handle \(P_{\text{rated}} = 4 \times 0.25\text{ W} = 1.0\text{ W} > 0.82\text{ W}\) (\(22\%\) thermal margin).
      • Thermal Dissipation: Distributes heat across 8 solder pads and copper planes, eliminating localized hot spots.
  • RF Output Coupling: Choke inductor \(\text{RFC} = [...]\ \mu\text{H}\) blocks RF from entering the DC rail; \(10\text{ nF}\) DC blocking capacitors are placed at the input and output.
  • Measurement: Spectrum output on CMU200 matched \(-50.0\text{ dBm}\) at \(\text{RBW} = 1\text{ MHz}\), confirming an integrated \(-40.0\text{ dBm}\) over \(30 - 40\text{ MHz}\).

docs.title: 3.4. LOG ENTRY #04: High-Side Power Switch (AO3401 P-MOS & 2N2222) & Gate Divider Debugging
docs.text:
• Control Objective: Gate the 15V supply via a 3.3V GPIO pin from a Raspberry Pi 5 to prevent thermal build-up and RF leakage during sky observations.
  • Switching Topology: High-side P-channel MOSFET (AO3401, \(V_{\text{DS,max}} = -30\text{V}\)) driven by a 2N2222 NPN level-shifter.
  • Debugging Gate Biasing:
    • Initial Fault: Initial breadboard test showed \(V_{\text{Source}} = 15\text{V}\) but \(V_{\text{Gate}} = 13\text{V}\) (\(V_{\text{GS}} = -2\text{V}\)), leaving the MOSFET in linear mode, generating high \(R_{\text{DS(on)}}\) and thermal drop.
    • Correction: Configured a balanced \(10\text{ k}\Omega - 10\text{ k}\Omega\) voltage divider between the 15V rail, AO3401 Gate, and 2N2222 Collector:
      • When \(\text{GPIO} = 0\text{V}\) (LOW): 2N2222 is cut off \(\implies V_G = 15\text{V}, V_{\text{GS}} = 0\text{V}\) (AO3401 fully OFF).
      • When \(\text{GPIO} = 3.3\text{V}\) (HIGH): 2N2222 saturates, dividing the gate voltage: $\(V_G = 15\text{V} \times \frac{10\text{k}\Omega}{10\text{k}\Omega + 10\text{k}\Omega} = 7.5\text{V} \implies V_{\text{GS}} = 7.5\text{V} - 15\text{V} = -7.5\text{V}\)$
      • \(V_{\text{GS}} = -7.5\text{V}\) guarantees deep saturation (\(R_{\text{DS(on)}} < 0.05\ \Omega\)) while staying safely within the absolute maximum gate limit (\(V_{\text{GS,max}} = \pm 12\text{V}\)) of the AO3401.

docs.title: 3.5. LOG ENTRY #05: Prototyping & Altium Designer 2-Layer PCB Implementation
docs.text:
• Handmade Prototype Evaluation: Deadbug/perfboard wiring validated DC biasing, current clamping, and MMIC gain staging. However, long component leads induced parasitic inductance and lacked environmental shielding.
  • Altium Designer 2-Layer PCB Rules:
    • Layer Stackup: Standard FR-4, thickness \(H = 1.6\text{ mm}\), copper weight \(1\text{ oz}\) (\(35\ \mu\text{m}\)).
    • Continuous Ground Plane: The Bottom Layer is reserved as a \(100\%\) solid, unbroken ground plane. No signal traces cross the bottom layer beneath the GALI-74 or the RF path to preserve return current loops.
    • \(50\ \Omega\) RF Transmission Line: Calculated coplanar waveguide / microstrip geometry:
      • Trace width (\(W\)): \([...]\text{ mm}\).
      • Ground gap (\(S\)): \([...]\text{ mm}\).
    • RF Connector: Board-edge SMA female receptacle (Edge-Mount) soldered across both top signal and bottom ground planes.
    • Via Stitching: Array of ground vias placed at \([...]\text{ mm}\) pitch along the RF boundary to suppress ground loop impedance.

docs.text:
Figure 7.1: Complete circuit schematic of the gated avalanche noise source. Figure 7.2: PCB Top Layer layout showing the \(4 \times 510\ \Omega\) parallel bank and \(50\ \Omega\) RF trace.

Figure 7.3: PCB Bottom Layer layout demonstrating the continuous unbroken ground plane.

Figure 7.4: 3D isometric visualization of the fully assembled PCB module.

docs.title: 3.6. LOG ENTRY #06: End-to-End System Integration & Correlator Validation
docs.text:
• Test Topology: The fabricated noise source was routed through a Mini-Circuits 1:2 symmetric splitter into Port C of both SDRplay RSPdx receivers. Both SDRs shared a common 24 MHz reference clock via REFin.
  • Execution: Executed the real-time time-alignment pipeline (alignment_test) on Raspberry Pi 5:
====================================================================================
NOISE SOURCE HARDWARE STATE      MEASURED PNR     CORRELATION BEHAVIOR / OUTCOME
====================================================================================
ACTIVE / ON  (GPIO = HIGH)         44.0 dB        Sharp Dirac delta spike; locks k = 0
INACTIVE/OFF (GPIO = LOW)          26.0 dB        Thermal / ADC quantization floor
====================================================================================
  • State ON (\(\text{PNR} = 44\text{ dB}\)): High correlated broadband power eliminates multi-peak ambiguities, enabling the \(\arg\max\) algorithm to resolve \(k_{\text{offset}}\) instantaneously with zero sample jitter.
  • State OFF (\(\text{PNR} = 26\text{ dB}\)): The AO3401 P-MOS switch fully decouples the 15V supply, dropping inter-channel correlation to ambient background noise and proving adequate RF isolation.

docs.text: ⚠️ **Status: In Progress

docs.title: 1.1. Role of the RF Switching Matrix in the 2-Element Solar Interferometer
docs.text:
In a two-element radio interferometer observing decametric solar radio bursts across the 30.0 – 40.0 MHz band, instrumental phase coherence and delay stability between the dual receive channels are critical. The physical system captures celestial radio emissions via two spatially separated antennas and feeds them into two independent SDRplay RSPdx receivers operating at a center frequency of 35.0 MHz with a 10.0 MSPS sample rate, interfaced to a Raspberry Pi 5 edge processor over USB 3.0 links.

To enable real-time interferometric correlation, the digital backend requires automated calibration routines: 1. Coarse sample delay compensation (\(k_{\text{offset}} = 0\)) to align non-deterministic USB enumeration and driver startup latencies between the two digitizers. 2. Instrumental phase equalization (\(\Delta\phi_0(f)\)) across all frequency bins.

Performing calibration by manually reconnecting coaxial cables introduces mechanical wear, cable phase disturbances, and operational downtime. The Dual-Channel RF Switching Matrix integrates electronic routing and power splitting onto a single printed circuit board, routing either the dual sky antennas (Observation Mode) or a common broadband noise reference (Calibration Mode) into the receivers under direct software control.

docs.title: 1.2. Key Electrical Specifications
docs.text:
Parameter / Metric Target Specification Design Constraint / Basis Operating Passband 30.0 – 40.0 MHz Ionospheric window & 10 MSPS USB throughput limit Observation Insertion Loss (\(S_{21}\)) \(< 0.8\text{ dB}\) Cascaded Friis noise figure & receiver sensitivity preservation Observation Return Loss (\(S_{11}\)) \(\le -15.0\text{ dB}\) Standing wave suppression (\(\vert\Gamma\vert^2 \le 3.16\%\), \(\text{VSWR} < 1.43:1\)) Calibration Attenuation (\(S_{21}\)) \(\approx -6.3\text{ dB}\) 3-resistor \(50\ \Omega\) Delta divider theoretical split + FET loss Switch Off-State Isolation \(\ge 40.0\text{ dB}\) Software-controlled noise source DC power gating strategy Inter-Channel Gain Balance (\(\Delta \vert S_{21}\vert\)) \(< 0.2\text{ dB}\) FX Correlator fringe coherence & zero-delay locking (\(\Delta\phi \approx 0^\circ\))

📘 Detailed Derivations: For detailed mathematical proofs, RF loss budgets, and physics constraints supporting these targets, refer to Appendix A: RF Switch Specification Derivations & Design Constraints.

docs.title: 2.1.1. Evaluation of High-Speed SPDT MMIC Switches (GaAs HMC544A)
docs.text: The primary routing elements consist of two HMC544A GaAs MMIC Single-Pole Double-Throw (SPDT) switches in 6-lead SOT-23 packages. Operating from DC to 4.0 GHz, the HMC544A provides low insertion loss, high linearity, and sub-microsecond switching speeds. Compared to electromechanical relays, solid-state GaAs switches eliminate contact bounce, mechanical wear, and coil-induced electromagnetic pickup.

docs.title: 2.1.2. Direct 3.3V GPIO Logic Interfacing from Raspberry Pi 5
docs.text:
The HMC544A requires complementary control logic (\(V_1, V_2\)) to establish RF conduction paths: * State 0 (\(V_1 = 0\text{V},\ V_2 = 3.3\text{V}\)): RFC connected to RF1 (Sky Antenna Input).

  • State 1 (\(V_1 = 3.3\text{V},\ V_2 = 0\text{V}\)): RFC connected to RF2 (Calibration Splitter Input).

To switch both channels synchronously using a single GPIO line from the Raspberry Pi 5, an on-board single-gate inverter (74LVC1G04) generates the complementary logic drive, guaranteeing synchronized channel reconfiguration.

docs.title: 2.2.1. 3-Resistor Delta (Δ) Configuration Using 50Ω Standard Resistors
docs.text: The calibration reference port (CAL IN) distributes incoming noise power symmetrically to the RF2 ports of Switch A and Switch B through an on-board 3-resistor Delta (\(\Delta\)) network. The network utilizes three standard \(50\ \Omega\) SMD resistors (\(1\%\) tolerance) connected in a closed delta topology between the input port and the two switch branches. This configuration provides wideband phase linearity and group delay stability across 30.0 – 40.0 MHz without reactive components, maintaining identical phase delivery to both receiver branches.

docs.title: 2.3. AC Coupling and DC Blocking Network
2.3.1. DC Blocking Capacitor Sizing (1nF SMD Ceramic Capacitors)
docs.text: Because the internal GaAs FET channels of the HMC544A operate at specific internal DC bias potentials, DC blocking capacitors are placed in series on all RF ports (RFC, RF1, and RF2). Ceramic surface-mount capacitors (\(1\text{ nF}\), 0603, C0G/NP0 dielectric) are implemented. At \(35.0\text{ MHz}\), a \(1\text{ nF}\) capacitance exhibits a reactance of \(X_C \approx 4.55\ \Omega\), yielding a high-pass cutoff frequency of \(f_c \approx 3.18\text{ MHz}\) into a \(50\ \Omega\) termination, well below the 30.0 – 40.0 MHz band of interest.

docs.title: 2.4.1. Ultra-Low Capacitance Bidirectional ESD Protection Diodes
docs.text: Because the antenna elements are deployed outdoors, they are susceptible to electrostatic discharge (ESD) and atmospheric static accumulation. Bidirectional transient voltage suppressor (TVS) diodes with ultra-low junction capacitance (\(C_j < 0.5\text{ pF}\)) are placed across the Antenna A and Antenna B input lines directly adjacent to the SMA connectors. The high capacitive reactance of these diodes across 30.0 – 40.0 MHz ensures transparent RF operation without shunting high-frequency signal energy to ground.

docs.title: Technical Notes on Selected Components:
docs.text:
• Resistive Power Splitter Network (R3, R5, R6): The \(49.9\ \Omega\) value corresponds to the nearest standard EIA E96 1% precision resistor rating for nominal \(50.0\ \Omega\), maintaining accurate port matching and equal power split with minimal reflection.
  • ESD Clamping Diodes (D2 – D6): The Texas Instruments TPD1E01B04 features an ultra-low typical capacitance of \(0.18\text{ pF}\), making it transparent across the 30.0 – 40.0 MHz band without degrading return loss or adding phase distortion.
  • Polarity & Header Security (D1, J1): The SS14 Schottky diode guards the active ICs against reverse supply connections, while the industrial screw terminal (KF128-5.08-3P) provides secure field wiring to the Raspberry Pi 5 GPIO lines and power rails.

docs.text:

docs.title: 3.2.1. PCB Stackup, 50 Ω Transmission Line Synthesis & Via Shielding
docs.text: To preserve impedance matching and phase balance across 30.0 – 40.0 MHz, all high-frequency signal lines are designed for a nominal characteristic impedance of \(Z_0 = 50.0\ \Omega\).

docs.title: 1. Substrate & CPW-G Synthesis (Saturn PCB Toolkit)
docs.text:
A Coplanar Waveguide with Ground (CPW-G) geometry was synthesized on a standard 2-layer FR-4 substrate (Kingboard KB-6164) using the 2D Field Solver in Saturn PCB Toolkit:

Following the layout phase, the switching matrix prototype was fabricated on a standard 1.6 mm 2-layer FR-4 substrate.

docs.title: 4.1. Vector Network Analyzer Test Setup (30.0 – 40.0 MHz Calibration)
docs.text:
To validate the high-frequency performance and port tracking of the fabricated RF Switching Matrix, laboratory measurements were conducted using a calibrated two-port Vector Network Analyzer (VNA). Prior to measurement, a standard Short-Open-Load-Through (SOLT) calibration was performed across 1.0 – 200.0 MHz to shift the measurement reference planes directly to the end faces of the coaxial test cables.

The assembled board (DUT) was powered with a 3.3V DC supply, and the RF routing state was set via the control pin. During each two-port transmission (\(S_{21}\)) and reflection (\(S_{11}\)) measurement sweep, all unused/idle RF ports were terminated with precision \(50\ \Omega\) broadband dummy loads to prevent parasitic reflections and preserve system impedance matching.

Figure 4.1: Laboratory measurement setup connecting the Device Under Test (DUT) to the Vector Network Analyzer

docs.title: 4.4.1. Observation Mode Transmission & Port Match (Antenna paths)
docs.text: In Observation Mode, both transmission paths exhibit low insertion loss and good impedance matching across the 30.0 – 40.0 MHz frequency window: * Insertion Loss (\(S_{21}\)): Across the target band, the measured forward transmission remains stable at \(S_{21} \approx -0.45\text{ dB}\) on both Antenna A \(\to\) OUT A (Figure 4.3) and Antenna B \(\to\) OUT B (Figure 4.9). This minimal attenuation satisfies the initial requirement (\(< 0.8\text{ dB}\)), preserving receiver sensitivity and preventing front-end noise figure degradation. * Return Loss (\(S_{11}\)): The input return loss remains below \(-18.0\text{ dB}\) (\(\text{VSWR} \approx 1.28:1\)), confirming that the coplanar waveguide routing and SMA launch transitions maintain \(50\ \Omega\) characteristic impedance.

docs.title: 4.4.2. Calibration Mode Power Division & Flatness (Noise Source paths)
docs.text: When switched to Calibration Mode, the external noise reference is distributed via the internal Delta resistive network: * Forward Coupling (\(S_{21}\)): Measured forward transmission is \(S_{21} \approx -6.3\text{ dB}\) to both OUT A (Figure 4.4) and OUT B (Figure 4.6). This closely matches theoretical expectations: \(-6.02\text{ dB}\) nominal power division from the 3-resistor \(50\ \Omega\) Delta configuration plus \(\approx 0.35\text{ dB}\) switch on-state path loss. * Band Flatness: The transmission curve exhibits less than \(0.15\text{ dB}\) peak-to-peak ripple across the 10 MHz passband with linear phase behavior, preventing distortion of injected reference noise. * Port Match (\(S_{11}\)): Calibration input return loss measures better than \(-20\text{ dB}\), preventing reflections back into the noise generator.

docs.title: 4.4.3. Off-State Switch Isolation
docs.text:
• Antenna Isolation (Calibration Mode): When observing paths are deactivated (Figures 4.3 and 4.9), off-state isolation reaches \(-67\text{ dB}\) to \(-68\text{ dB}\), with \(S_{11}\) approaching \(0\text{ dB}\) (purely reactive reflective state), preventing external interference from entering during calibration.
  • Noise Source Isolation (Observation Mode): Isolation between the inactive calibration splitter and the receiver outputs measures \(\approx -58\text{ dB}\) (Figures 4.5 and 4.7). Because the avalanche noise source DC bias is actively cut during observation, total noise leakage drops below the sky background floor (\(< -120\text{ dBm}\)), validating the relaxed isolation strategy.

docs.title: 4.4.4. Dual-Channel Tracking & Symmetry Verification
docs.text:
• Amplitude Balance: The inter-channel gain delta between Path A and Path B satisfies: $\(\Delta |S_{21}| = \big| |S_{21,\text{Path A}}| - |S_{21,\text{Path B}}| \big| < 0.15\text{ dB}\)$
  • Phase Alignment: Due to symmetric trace routing and length matching (\(\Delta L < 0.2\text{ mm}\)), the differential phase offset remains negligible (\(\Delta\phi \approx 0^\circ\)), ensuring baseline symmetry for the correlation engine.

docs.title: 5.1. GPIO Switching Logic from Raspberry Pi 5
docs.text:
The RF Switching Matrix operates in tandem with the active power gate of the avalanche noise source via two dedicated Raspberry Pi 5 GPIO commands:

Operating Mode GPIO 1 (GPIO_SW) GPIO 2 (GPIO_NOISE) RF Switch Position Noise Source DC Power Correlator Function Observation LOW (0V) LOW (0V) Antenna → Receiver OUT OFF (0V, Gated) Solar Fringe Acquisition (Module 3) Calibration HIGH (3.3V) HIGH (3.3V) Noise Splitter → Receiver OUT ON (+15V, Active) Delay & Phase Locking (Module 2)

Figure 5.1: Dual-state control sequence and signal timing diagram

Cutting DC power to the noise source during observation guarantees that no broadband noise leaks into the receiver front-ends, validating the relaxed switch isolation strategy.

docs.title: 5.2. Digital Backend Delay Alignment Verification (k=0 Lock)
docs.text:
To verify end-to-end hardware symmetry, the switching matrix was tested in Calibration Mode using the backend alignment engine (Module 2). Broadband noise injected through the Delta splitter was ingested simultaneously by both RSPdx receivers.

The backend computes the cross-correlation function via FFTW3:

\[ R_{12}[k] = \mathcal{F}^{-1}\left\{ \mathcal{F}\{\tilde{x}_1[n]\} \cdot \mathcal{F}^*\{\tilde{x}_2[n]\} \right\} \]

Due to the length-matched CPW-G traces and symmetric \(50\ \Omega\) Delta divider network, the cross-correlation collapses into an isolated Dirac peak locked deterministically at lag index \(k = 0\) with a high Peak-to-Noise Ratio (\(\text{PNR} > 20\text{ dB}\)), verifying zero inter-channel hardware timing skew.

docs.title: 6. Chapter Summary
docs.text: The design, CAD layout, and laboratory verification of the Dual-Channel RF Switching Matrix provide an automated front-end routing solution for the 30.0 – 40.0 MHz solar interferometer. Utilizing GaAs MMIC switches, a symmetric \(50\ \Omega\) Delta resistive power divider, \(1\text{ nF}\) DC blocking capacitors, and low-capacitance ESD protection, the board delivers balanced dual-channel routing. Coordinating switch logic with active noise source power gating ensures reliable isolation, while digital backend testing confirms zero-delay (\(k=0\)) sample alignment across the receive chain.

docs.title: System Architecture and Master Orchestrator
docs.text:
This document specifies the process model, synchronization contract, DSP data path, output interfaces, and failure policy of the Solar Radio Interferometer. The target system uses a Raspberry Pi 5 and two SDRplay RSPdx receivers, with a nominal complex-sampled RF interval of 30–40 MHz.

Implementation baseline: ad810d5364a2a10ef51be5429cdf0a49234edcb4. The supplied main(1).cpp is byte-identical to src/main.cpp at this revision. Descriptions below refer to this baseline and the checked-in configuration. Runtime timing, physical switch settling, RF calibration accuracy and installed SDK behavior require deployment measurements; source inspection does not certify those properties.

docs.title: 1.1 System block diagram
docs.text:
Figure 1 presents the complete signal path and the software blocks that control it. Solid arrows carry RF signals, I/Q samples or spectral products. Dashed arrows carry control commands. The RF switching block represents the two-channel antenna/calibration selection function, rather than a component-level wiring schematic.

flowchart TD
    subgraph RF["RF inputs and calibration path"]
        A1["Antenna CH1"] --> SW["Two-channel RF source selection"]
        A2["Antenna CH2"] --> SW
        NS["Common noise source and splitter"] --> SW
    end

    SW --> RX1["RSPdx CH1: 35 MHz, 10 MSPS"]
    SW --> RX2["RSPdx CH2: 35 MHz, 10 MSPS"]

    subgraph PI["Raspberry Pi 5: acquisition and processing"]
        C1["Producer process CH1"] --> R1["SHM ring CH1: 16 MiB payload"]
        C2["Producer process CH2"] --> R2["SHM ring CH2: 16 MiB payload"]
        R1 --> PRE["Startup alignment and optional phase calibration"]
        R2 --> PRE
        PRE --> FX["Welch FX correlator: FFT, cross and auto spectra"]
        M["main.cpp: master supervisor"] -.->|"Start, monitor, stop"| C1
        M -.->|"Start, monitor, stop"| C2
        M -.->|"Sequence and supervise"| PRE
        M -.->|"Run integration cycles"| FX
    end

    RX1 -->|"USB: I/Q samples"| C1
    RX2 -->|"USB: I/Q samples"| C2
    M -.->|"GPIO 6: source selection"| SW
    M -.->|"GPIO 26: noise control"| NS

    FX --> UDP["SOL2 v3 UDP: five spectral products"]
    UDP --> VIEW["Receiving client or viewer"]
    FX --> STORE["Optional storage queue and worker"]
    STORE --> H5["Rolling HDF5 files and SQLite ledger"]

Figure 1. System-level signal and control architecture. RF source selection feeds two independent receiver/producer paths; paired sample consumption produces live telemetry and optional scientific archives.

The two acquisition paths remain separate through the SHM rings. The parent consumes paired samples, establishes the startup alignment/calibration state and then repeatedly runs the correlator. The startup block describes a lifecycle phase, not a separate process or an alignment filter executed on every integration. The master supervisor controls acquisition and processing; it is not an additional sample-copy stage.

The processing chain is RF selection → dual acquisition → shared-memory buffering → paired DSP → telemetry and storage. Alignment preserves a relative integer-sample relationship between channels; the software stream gates do not act as a hardware trigger. The detailed process topology in Section 2 and Welch dataflow in Section 4 expand the corresponding blocks of this overview.

docs.title: 1.2 Master supervisor and consumer
docs.text:
main() is the lifecycle and data-publication coordinator. It validates command-line options, acquires a single-instance lock, discovers receiver serial numbers, launches two acquisition processes, attaches to their shared-memory buffers, initializes DSP and output resources, performs startup alignment and optional phase calibration, and supervises continuous integration. It also coordinates GPIO commands and orderly termination.

The orchestration connects four functional domains:

  1. Acquisition: SDRplay callbacks in one producer process per receiver.
  2. Startup conditioning: sample alignment and optional static phase calibration.
  3. Correlation: the FXCorrelator consumer operating on both sample streams.
  4. Publication: UDP telemetry and an optional storage pipeline.

This grouping is an architectural organization of the visible calls, not a claim about the repository's module numbering. Signal-processing algorithms reside behind included interfaces; main.cpp primarily establishes their ordering and operating conditions.

Design rationale. Separating acquisition from the consumer permits receiver callbacks to continue while the parent performs integration and publication. Shared-memory buffers decouple short-term producer/consumer scheduling differences. This does not establish hard real-time behavior or unlimited tolerance to consumer stalls.
